:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying a Quadratic Form Type by Calculating the Corresponding Eigenvalues

:question/problem:
Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{aligned}].$ Which of the following statements are true?

- The eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=7$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=10$
- ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is positive-definite
- $A$ is indefinite
:question/worked-solution:
Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}9-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & -6-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (9-\lambda )(-6-\lambda )-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -70 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-7,\,10.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. Since $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is indefinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying a Quadratic Form Type Using Sylvester's Criterion

:question/problem:
Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 6\end{aligned}].$ Which of the following statements are true?

- ${a}_{11}=9$ and $det(A)=18$
- ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is positive-definite
- $A$ is negative-definite
:question/worked-solution:
Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=9$ and 

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 6\end{aligned}|=18.
$$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=9>0, \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 6\end{aligned}|=18>0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are positive-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying a Quadratic Form Type Using Sylvester's Criterion

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: None of the statements are true

:question/problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ shown above.
Which of the following statements are true?

- ${a}_{11}=-1$ and $det(A)>0$
- ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is negative-definite
- $A$ is positive-definite
:question/worked-solution:
Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=-1$ but 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -6\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot 2 \\  & =-4<0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-1<0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -6\end{aligned}|=2>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=-4<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are negative-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements Regarding Properties of Symmetric Matrices

:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true? 

- If $A$ is *any* matrix, then $A{A}^{T}$ is always symmetric.
- The sum of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.
- The product of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.
:question/worked-solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A{A}^{T})^{T} & =({A}^{T})^{T}{A}^{T} \\  & =A{A}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}+{B}^{T} \\  & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. As a counterexample, consider the symmetric matrices 

$\,$ $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

However, their product is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements Regarding Properties of Symmetric Matrices

:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- If $A$ is *any*  $n\times n$  matrix, then $A-{A}^{T}$ is always symmetric.
- The sum of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.
- If $A$ is symmetric, then ${A}^{-1}$ is always symmetric (if it exists).
:question/worked-solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. As a counterexample, consider the matrix 

$\,$ $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$

However, $A-{A}^{T}$ is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{A}^{T} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}+{B}^{T} \\  & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any non-singular symmetric matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}({A}^{-1})^{T} & =({A}^{T})^{-1} \\  & ={A}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Conservative Vector Fields

:question/problem:
Which of the following vector fields are conservative on ${R}^{2}?$

- $F=x{e}^{xy}\,i+y{e}^{xy}\,j$
- $G=(xy+{y}^{2})\,i+(xy+{x}^{2})\,j$
- $H=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\,j$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j$ be a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$F$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

Note that for each of our functions, $D={R}^{2}.$ With this in mind, let's check each of the vector fields. 

- For the vector field $F,$ we have $P=x{e}^{xy}$ and $Q=y{e}^{xy}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}={x}^{2}{e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are not equal, we conclude that $F$ is not conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $G,$ we have $P=xy+{y}^{2}$ and $Q=xy+{x}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x+2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y+2x.
$$

Since the partial derivatives are not equal, we conclude that $G$ is not conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $H,$ we have $P=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)$ and $Q=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y).$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y),\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y).
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $H$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field by Identifying Asymptotic Behavior

:question/problem:
![](images/1b/1b608fabe99c6062f9d9f04cc7f3b2933e453812ed4ce9783908666c71c1c74b.png)

Which of the following equations could have generated the slope field shown above?

I. ${y}^{′}=\frac{y}{y-1}$
II. ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{y}$
III. ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}$
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/7b/7bb52825944a7515a6281a88b5bc740cf6d097380fa13fe7e00efc5e499d49f8.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- The slopes of the slope field become vertical as $y\to 0.$

- The slopes of the slope field become horizontal as $y\to \pm \infty .$

- The slopes of the slope field are positive everywhere.

With that in mind, let's consider each equation.

- The equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{y}{y-1}$ does *not* give the required behavior. Notice that

$$
\frac{y}{y-1}=\frac{1}{(1-\frac{1}{y})}\to 1\,\text{as}\,y\to \pm \infty .
$$

Therefore, the slopes of the slope field for this differential equation do not become horizontal as $y\to \pm \infty .$

- The equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{y}$ does *not* give the required behavior. The slopes of the slope field for this differential equation are negative for $y<0.$

- The equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}$ gives the required behavior. Notice that ${y}^{′}\to 0$ as $y\to \infty ,$ and ${y}^{′}\to \infty $ as $y\to 0.$ Also, the right-hand side of this equation is positive for all $y\ne 0.$

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field Using the Sign of the Slopes and Factoring

:question/problem:
![](images/bb/bba667daa6bfd40eeb5450cc86066184819b903ace2641bc58c6b5c83869a4b6.png)

Which of the following equations could have generated the slope field shown above?

- ${y}^{′}={y}^{2}-2y$
- ${y}^{′}={y}^{2}-4y+4$
- ${y}^{′}=2y-{y}^{2}$
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/72/72801ec62e5e23173097ef674169b26c85fab65cbf543af44b3582f0e14fd0c4.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slope field is zero along the lines $y=0$ and $y=2.$ Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should evaluate to zero on both of these lines.

- Second, the lines $y=0$ and $y=2$ divide the plane into $3$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $3$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| Region | $y<0$ | $0<y<2$ | $y>2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↗$ | $↘$ | $↗$ |
| Sign | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

With that in mind, let's consider each equation.

- The equation 

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-2y=y(y-2)
$$

gives the required behavior.

- The equation

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{2}-4y+4=(y-2)^{2}
$$

does *not* give the required behavior. The right-hand side evaluates to zero at $y=2$ only.

- The equation 

$$
{y}^{′}=2y-{y}^{2}=y(2-y)
$$

does *not* give the required behavior. The right-hand side evaluates to zero at $y=0$ and $y=2,$ but the sign of the slopes in the required regions (summarized below) do not correspond to the given slope field.

| Region | $y<0$ | $0<y<2$ | $y>2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↘$ | $↗$ | $↘$ |
| Sign | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ |

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field by Identifying Asymptotic Behavior

:question/problem:
![](images/66/660feebe44e179b53be85d23c497e58de4774258b588a6f8ac785a0fd9c8fc08.png)

Which of the following equations could have generated the slope field shown above?

- ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{2y-{y}^{2}-1}$
- ${y}^{′}=-\frac{{y}^{2}+y}{y-1}$
- ${y}^{′}=\frac{3}{y-1}$
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/a7/a76856ea0a6b50b821ba6c39e6a87a5acf5aabd704454b4875540b3970f3d249.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- The slopes of the slope field become vertical as $y\to 1.$

- The slopes of the slope field become horizontal as $y\to \pm \infty .$

- The slopes of the slope field are negative everywhere.

With that in mind, let's consider each equation.

- The equation 

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{1}{2y-{y}^{2}-1}=-\frac{1}{(y-1)^{2}}
$$

gives the required behavior. Notice that ${y}^{′}\to 0$ as $y\to \infty ,$ and ${y}^{′}\to \infty $ as $y\to 1.$ Also, the right-hand side of this equation is negative for all $y\ne 1.$

- The equation ${y}^{′}=-\frac{{y}^{2}+y}{y-1}$ does *not* give the required behavior. Notice that

$$
-\frac{{y}^{2}+y}{y-1}=-\frac{y+1}{(1-\frac{1}{y})}\to ∓\infty \,\text{as}\,y\to \pm \infty .
$$

Therefore, the slopes of the slope field for this differential equation do not become horizontal as $y\to \pm \infty .$

- The equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{3}{y-1}$ does *not* give the required behavior. The slopes of the slope field for this differential equation are positive for $y>1.$

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying a Decoupled System of Linear ODEs

:question/problem:
Which of the following systems of linear ODEs are decoupled?

- ${x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t)$
- ${x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)$
- ${x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]x(t)$
:question/worked-solution:
A *decoupled system* consists of equations depending on only one variable, such as

$$
{x}_{i}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{i}{x}_{i}(t),
$$

where ${\lambda }_{i}$ is a constant. This means that we can solve each equation independently. 

In matrix form, a linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ is decoupled if $A$ is a diagonal matrix.

With this in mind, let's examine our systems.

- Systems I and III are decoupled since their corresponding matrices are diagonal.

- System II is *not* decoupled because its matrix is not diagonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying a Decoupled System of Linear ODEs

:question/problem:
Which of the following systems of linear ODEs are decoupled?

- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}$
- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=\pi {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}$
- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}$
:question/worked-solution:
A *decoupled system* consists of equations depending on only one variable, such as

$$
{x}_{i}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{i}{x}_{i}(t),
$$

where ${\lambda }_{i}$ is a constant. This means that we can solve each equation independently. 

With this in mind, let's examine our systems.

- Systems I is *not* decoupled because some of its equations depend on more than one variable. For example, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$

- System II is decoupled since its equations depend on only one variable each. Indeed, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{2}(t).$

- Systems III is *not* decoupled because some of its equations depend on more than one variable. For example, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Constructing General Solutions of First-Order Linear Systems of ODEs

:question/problem:
Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ satisfy the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t)$ and ${x}_{p}(t)$ satisfy the inhomogeneous system
${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t)+f(t).$
Which of the following is **always** a solution of the same inhomogeneous system?

- $3\cdot {x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$
- ${x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)+2\cdot {x}_{p}(t)$
- $-4\cdot {x}_{2}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if ${x}_{h}(t)$ satisfies a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution to an inhomogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ then ${x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$ is also a solution to the same inhomogeneous system.

Additonally, the *linearity principle* for systems of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) states that if ${x}_{1}(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t),…,{x}_{k}(t)$ are solutions to a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ then any linear combination 

$$
{c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)+⋯+{c}_{k}{x}_{k}(t)
$$

with ${c}_{1},{c}_{2},…,{c}_{k}\in R$ is also a solution of the same homogeneous system. 

With that in mind, let's examine the given expression.

- Option I is a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Indeed, notice that the linear combination 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)=3\cdot {x}_{1}(t)
$$

is a solution to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ according to the linearity principle. Thus, 

$$
{{3\cdot {x}_{1}(t)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{h}(t)}+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

is a solution to our inhomogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t).$

- Option II might be *not* a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that ${x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)+2\cdot {x}_{p}(t)$ can't be written as 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),
$$

where ${x}_{h}(t)$ is a solution of the homogeneous system, because of the multiplier $2$ next to the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$

- Option III is a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Indeed, notice that the linear combination 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)=-4\cdot {x}_{2}(t)
$$

is a solution to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ according to the linearity principle. Thus, 

$$
{{-4\cdot {x}_{2}(t)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{h}(t)}+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

is a solution to our inhomogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Applying the Linearity Principle to the Solutions of a Homogeneous System of ODEs

:question/problem:
Suppose ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are both solutions of the homogeneous system
${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t).$
Which of the following is **always** a solution of the same system?

- $x(t)={e}^{t}\,{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)$
- $x(t)={x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)$
- $x(t)={x}_{1}(t)\times {x}_{2}(t)$ (cross-product)
:question/worked-solution:
The *linearity principle* for systems of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) states that if ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are solutions to a homogeneous linear system, then for any constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ the linear combination 

$$
{c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)
$$

is also a solution of the system. 

With that in mind, let's examine the given expressions.

- Option I might be *not* a solution to the system since it's not a linear combination of the solutions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ Notice that the multiplier of the first term is not a constant.

- Option II is a solution to the system. Indeed, notice that

$$
{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)
$$

is a linear combination of the solutions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ with constant multiplies ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=1,$ respectively.

- Option III might be *not* a solution to the system since it's not a linear combination of the solutions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function

:question/problem:
Let $F(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $\pi $-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $f(x+\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$
- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$
- $f(x+\frac{5\pi }{2})=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $f$ is the $\pi $-periodic extension of $F,$ we have 

- $f(x+\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,\pi ).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $\pi $-periodicity: 

$$
f(x+\pi )=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is true. Notice that $F$ itself is $\pi $-periodic, because for any $x\in R,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x+\pi )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(x+\pi ))=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+2\pi )=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)=F(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $F$ already satisfies the periodicity rule, the $\pi $-periodic extension agrees with $F$ everywhere, so $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R.$

- Statement III is false. Since $f$ is $\pi $-periodic, shifting by $2\pi $ does not change the value of $f,$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x+\frac{5\pi }{2})=f((x+\frac{\pi }{2})+2\pi )=f(x+\frac{\pi }{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

But $f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})$ does not always equal $f(x).$ For example, take $x=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(\frac{5\pi }{6})=F(\frac{5\pi }{6})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3})=F(\frac{\pi }{3})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x+\frac{5\pi }{2})\ne f(x)$ for $x=\frac{\pi }{4}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Conservative Vector Fields

:question/problem:
Which of the following vector fields are conservative on ${R}^{2}?$

- $F=({x}^{2}+2y)\,i+({x}^{2}+2y)\,j$
- $G=(y{e}^{x}+2)\,i+({e}^{x}+4y)\,j$
- $H=y\,i+x\,j$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j$ be a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$F$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

Note that for each of our functions, $D={R}^{2}.$ 

With this in mind, let's check each of the vector fields. 

- For the vector field $F,$ we have $P={x}^{2}+2y$ and $Q={x}^{2}+2y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the partial derivatives are not equal, we conclude that $F$ is not conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $G,$ we have $P=y{e}^{x}+2$ and $Q={e}^{x}+4y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}={e}^{x},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $G$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

- For the vector field $H,$ we have $P=y$ and $Q=x.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $H$ is conservative on ${R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Equilibrium Solutions of a Differential Equation

:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-{y}^{2}=2y+{y}^{3}.$ Which of the following is an equilibrium solution of this equation?

- $y=0$
- $y=1$
- $y=2$
:question/worked-solution:
Given an autonomous differential equation ${y}^{′}(x)=f(y),$ if there exists a constant $c$ such that $f(c)=0,$ then $y=c$ is an equilibrium solution of the equation.

First, we write the given equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={y}^{3}+{y}^{2}+2y,
$$

and we get that $f(y)={y}^{3}+{y}^{2}+2y.$

Now, let's check each proposed solution by substituting them into $f(y).$

- $y=0$ is an equilibrium point. We have $f(0)={0}^{3}+{0}^{2}+2(0)=0.$$\,✓$

- $y=1$ is *not* an equilibrium point. We have $f(1)={1}^{3}+{1}^{2}+2(1)=4\ne 0.$ $\,\times $

- $y=2$ is *not* an equilibrium point. We have $f(2)={2}^{3}+{2}^{2}+2(2)=16\ne 0.$  $\,\times $

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements About Equilibrium Solutions

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: None of the statements are true

:question/problem:
Consider the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={y}^{3}-7y+6.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- ${y}_{1}(x)=1$ is an equilibrium solution of the equation
- The equation has $3$ distinct equilibrium solutions, ${y}_{1}(x),{y}_{2}(x),$ and ${y}_{3}(x)$
- ${y}_{1}(x)+{y}_{2}(x)+{y}_{3}(x)=0$
:question/worked-solution:
Given an autonomous differential equation ${y}^{′}(x)=f(y),$ if there exists a constant $c$ such that $f(c)=0,$ then $y=c$ is an equilibrium solution of the equation.

In our case, we have that $f(y)={y}^{3}-7y+6.$

Let's examine the statement one-by-one.

- Statement I is true.  We have that $f(1)={1}^{3}-7(1)+6=0.$

- Statement II is true. We know that $y=1$ is a solution to $f(y)=0,$ and so $(y-1)$ is a factor of the polynomial $f(y).$ Dividing $f(y)$ by $(y-1)$ using synthetic division, we get

|  | ${y}^{3}$ | ${y}^{2}$ | ${y}^{1}$ | ${y}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-7$ | $6$ |
|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-6$ |
|  | $1$ | $1$ | $-6$ | $0$ |

 
Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =(y-1)({y}^{2}+y-6) \\  & =(y-1)(y-2)(y+3)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(y)$ has three distinct equilibrium solutions, 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=1,\,{y}_{2}(x)=2,\,{y}_{3}(x)=-3.
$$

- Statement III is true. We have ${y}_{1}(x)+{y}_{2}(x)+{y}_{3}(x)=1+2+(-3)=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying the Order of an Ordinary Differential Equation

Which of the following are third-order ordinary differential equations?

- ${y}^{‴}+3x{y}^{′}=xy$
- $3{y}^{″}{y}^{′}-2xy=2{y}^{′}$
- ${x}^{3}{y}^{′}-2x={y}^{″}$
:question/worked-solution:
A differential equation is of third-order if the largest derivative term in the equation is ${y}^{‴}.$

Keeping this in mind, let's check each given equation.

- Equation I is a third-order differential equation. The highest derivative in this equation is ${y}^{‴}.$

- Equation II is not a third-order differential equation. The highest derivative in this equation is ${y}^{″},$ so this is a second-order differential equation.

- Equation III is not a third-order differential equation. The highest derivative in this equation is ${y}^{″},$ so this is a second-order differential equation.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Determining Whether an Ordinary Differential Equation is Autonomous or Nonautonomous

:question/problem:
Which of the following are autonomous ordinary differential equations?

- $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{y}$
- $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=0$
- $2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-xy=\sqrt{x}$
:question/worked-solution:
An ordinary differential equation with dependent variable $y$ and independent variable $x$ is said to be autonomous if it can be written in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ or equivalently, ${y}^{′}=f(y).$

With that in mind, let's check each of the differential equations:

- Equation I is an autonomous differential equation. We see that it is of the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ where $f(y)={e}^{y}.$

- Equation II is an autonomous differential equation. Writing the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=3y.$

- Equation III is not an autonomous differential equation. If we isolate the derivative term, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-xy & =\sqrt{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2}(xy+\sqrt{x}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}(xy+\sqrt{x}).$ So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Initial Value Problems and Initial Conditions

:question/problem:
Which of the following systems is a first-order initial value problem?

- $2x{y}^{′}=y,\,y(0)=1$
- ${y}^{′}-2xy={e}^{y}$
- $2x{y}^{″}={y}^{′},\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1$
:question/worked-solution:
A first-order initial value problem (or IVP) is a first-order ordinary differential equation together with an initial condition that specifies a value of the unknown function at a point in its domain. A first-order initial value problem typically takes the form

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y({x}_{0})={y}_{0},
$$

where ${x}_{0}$ and ${y}_{0}$ are constants.

With that in mind, let's check each option.

- System I is a first-order initial value problem. It consists of a first-order differential equation $2x{y}^{′}=y$ together with the initial condition $y(0)=1.$

- System II is not a first-order initial value problem. We have a first-order ordinary differential equation, but there is no initial condition.

- System III is not a first-order initial value problem. It consists of a *second*-order differential equation $2x{y}^{″}={y}^{′}$ together with *two* initial conditions $y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1.$ This is a second-order initial value problem.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field Using the Sign of the Slopes

:question/problem:
![](images/76/76c15fa584f5a216d23ef10b10fbae14c09b84714e49bd8db0cc7954cab8c0f3.png)

![](images/11/111e679939475cabbfe9a40779de3fa1bf4f2de732f943a3b0396a3ee9bf3519.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes of the slope field are horizontal along the lines $x=0$ and $x=2.$ Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should evaluate to zero on both of these lines.

- Second, the lines $x=0$ and $x=2$ divide the plane into $3$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $3$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| Region | $x<0$ | $0<x<2$ | $x>2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↗$ | $↘$ | $↗$ |
| Sign | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

With that in mind, let's consider each equation.

- The equation ${y}^{′}=x(x-2)^{2}$ does *not* give the required behavior. The right-hand side evaluates to zero at $x=0$ and $x=2,$ but the sign of the slopes in the required regions (summarized below) do not correspond to the given slope field.

| Region | $x<0$ | $0<x<2$ | $x>2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↘$ | $↗$ | $↗$ |
| Sign | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |

- The equation ${y}^{′}=x(x-2)$ gives the required behavior.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying an Equation That Generates a Slope Field Using Asymptotes

:question/problem:
![](images/68/680bc0001fb95783ee70fc88a7106997bcb3dba2ad85a708164878d0f610ecfb.png)

Which of the following equations could have generated the slope field shown above?

- ${y}^{′}=x(x-2)$
- ${y}^{′}=\frac{5x}{x-2}$
- ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{x-2}$
:question/worked-solution:
![](images/74/74b482b5b72421c9ee208034dc4727605e42874015d080130ffd7d18437af0da.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- The solution curves have the vertical asymptote $x=2.$

- The slopes of the slope field become horizontal as $x\to \pm \infty .$

With that in mind, let's consider each equation.

- The equation ${y}^{′}=x(x-2)$ does *not* give the required behavior. The right-hand side does not approach $\pm \infty $ as $x\to 2.$

- The equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{5x}{x-2}$ does *not* give the required behavior. Notice that

$$
\frac{5x}{x-2}=\frac{5}{(1-\frac{2}{x})}\to 5\,\text{as}\,x\to \pm \infty .
$$

Therefore, the slopes of the slope field for this differential equation do not become horizontal as $x\to \pm \infty .$

- The equation ${y}^{′}=\frac{1}{x-2}$ gives the required behavior. Notice that

$$
\frac{1}{x-2}\to 0\,\text{as}\,x\to \pm \infty .
$$

Therefore, the slopes of the slope field for this differential equation become horizontal as $x\to \pm \infty .$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Determining Whether an Ordinary Differential Equation is Autonomous or Nonautonomous

:question/problem:
Which of the following are **not** autonomous ordinary differential equations?

- ${y}^{′}={e}^{x}$
- ${y}^{′}-\frac{3}{y}=0$
- $\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}-xy={e}^{x}$
:question/worked-solution:
An ordinary differential equation with dependent variable $y$ and independent variable $x$ is said to be autonomous if it can be written in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ or equivalently, ${y}^{′}=f(y).$

With that in mind, let's check each of the differential equations:

- Equation I is *not* an autonomous differential equation. It is not of the form ${y}^{′}=f(y).$

- Equation II is an autonomous differential equation. Writing the equation in the form ${y}^{′}=f(y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}-\frac{3}{y} & =0 \\ {y}^{′} & =\frac{3}{y} \\ {y}^{′} & =f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=\frac{3}{y}.$

- Equation III is *not* an autonomous differential equation. If we isolate the derivative term, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}-xy & ={e}^{x} \\ \frac{1}{2}{y}^{′} & =xy+{e}^{x} \\ {y}^{′} & =2(xy+{e}^{x}) \\ {y}^{′} & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)=2(xy+{e}^{x}).$ So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form ${y}^{′}=f(y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Vector Fields That Are Independent of Path

:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=⟨y,\,-x⟩$ and the points $O(0,0)$ and $A(1,1)$ in the $xy$-plane. 

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=0,$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the line segment $\overset{―}{OA},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$
- ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=0,$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the parabola $y={x}^{2},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$
- ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ is independent of path.
- $F$ is conservative.
:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

With that in mind, we consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Parameterizing the line segment, we have

$$
{r}_{1}(t)=⟨t,\,t⟩,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}⟨t,\,-t⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,1⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t-t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}0\,\text{d}t \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Parameterizing the line segment, we have

$$
{r}_{2}(t)=⟨t,\,{t}^{2}⟩,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}⟨{t}^{2},\,-t⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,2t⟩\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}-2{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ have the same initial and terminal points, yet

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r\ne {\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r,
$$

we conclude that ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r$ is path-dependent.

- Statement IV is false. If a vector field is conservative then it is path-independent. Since $F$ is path-dependent, it is not conservative.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Vector Fields That Are Independent of Path

:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{x+y},\,{e}^{x+y}⟩$ and the points $O(0,0)$ and $A(1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)$ in the $xy$-plane. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $F$ is conservative.

II. ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2e-1,$ where ${C}_{1}$ is the path along the line segment $\overset{―}{OA},$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$

III. ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2e-1,$ where ${C}_{2}$ is the path along the curve $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1),$ traversed from $O$ to $A.$
:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

With that in mind, we consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Notice that $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ with domain $D={R}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{x+y}.
$$

Since the partial derivatives exist and are continuous and equal everywhere on ${R}^{2},$ we conclude that $F$ is conservative.

- Statement II is true. Since $F$ is conservative, there exists a function $f$ such that $∇f=F.$ Reconstructing the function $f$ from its gradient in the usual way, we get

$$
f={e}^{x+y}.
$$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}∇f\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =f(1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2)-f(0,0) \\  & ={e}^{1+\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{0} \\  & =e\cdot {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-1 \\  & =2e-1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Since $F$ is conservative and ${C}_{2}$ has the same initial and terminal points as ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2e-1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

| $y>0$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $y<0$ | $+$ | $-$ |
|  | $x<0$ | $x>0$ |

- Equation II gives the required behavior. The right-hand side of ${y}^{′}=-xy$ evaluates to zero at $x=0$ and $y=0,$ and the sign of the slopes in the required regions (summarized below) correspond to the given slope field.

| $y>0$ | $+$ | $-$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $y<0$ | $-$ | $+$ |
|  | $x<0$ | $x>0$ |

- Equation III does *not* give the required behavior. The right-hand side of ${y}^{′}=x+1$ evaluates to zero at $x=-1$ only.

- At every point in the third quadrant, the slope of the slope field is positive
:question/worked-solution:
First, we define $f(x,y)=2xy.$ Then, our differential equation is $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y).$ 

Notice that $f(x,y)=0$ when $x=0$ or $y=0.$ The lines $x=0$ and $y=0$ divide the plane into the usual four quadrants.

If we compute the sign of $f(x,y)$ in each quadrant (by considering some test points, for example), we get the following:

![](images/6e/6ef852c9c15dc6f591119906abe479949f929edb6dc26f21588b4de545d02da2.png)

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement I is true. If $(x,y)$ is in the first quadrant, then according to our diagram, we have

$$
{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(x,y)}=f(x,y)>0.\,
$$

This implies that the slope of the slope field is positive for any point $(x,y)$ in the first quadrant.

- Statement II is false. If $(x,y)$ is in the second quadrant, then according to our diagram, we have

$$
{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(x,y)}=f(x,y)<0.\,
$$

This implies that the slope of the slope field is negative for any point $(x,y)$ in the second quadrant.

- Statement III is true. If $(x,y)$ is in the third quadrant, then according to our diagram, we have

$$
{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(x,y)}=f(x,y)>0.\,
$$

This implies that the slope of the slope field is positive for any point $(x,y)$ in the third quadrant.

- Curve IV is negatively oriented. The arrows indicate that the curve is traversed clockwise.

A connected *plane* region $D$ is simply connected if every simple closed curve in $D$ encloses only points in $D.$ In other words, the region does not contain any holes. Plane regions containing holes are not simply connected, since some simple closed curves cannot be contracted to a point:

![](images/c3/c3c3e7a60ff0dd917cf6c0b293dae7510e457a0455629add1c54cadac65248b7.png)

With that in mind, let's examine each of the regions:

- Region III is simply connected. This is a connected region that does not contain holes.

- Region IV is not simply connected. Instead, this is a region that consists of two pieces (it's not connected).

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements Regarding Linear Transformations in the Cartesian Plane

:question/problem:
Consider a linear transformation $T$ that maps ${R}^{2}$ to the origin. Which of the following statements are true?

- $\text{rank}(T)=1$,  where $T$ is the standard matrix of $T$
- $\text{Im}(T)$ contains no vectors of ${R}^{2}$
- $\text{Ker}(T)={R}^{2}$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $T$ in ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T$ is the zero-subspace ${0},$ then

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=0
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-0 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. In our case, we have 

$$
\text{rank}(T)=0.
$$

- Statement II is false. The image of $T$ contains the vector zero vector $0=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the condition $\text{nullity}(T)=2$ in ${R}^{2}$ is equivalent to 

$$
\text{Ker}(T)={R}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Applying the Extreme Value Theorem to Piecewise Functions

:question/problem:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is defined as

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}x-1, & x<0.5 \\ 4-{x}^{2}, & x\ge 0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

On which of the following intervals can the extreme value theorem be applied to the function?

- $(0,1)$
- $[0,2]$
- $[1,2]$
:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the extreme value theorem is only applicable to closed intervals on which the function is continuous.

So, let's check whether the function is continuous on each of the intervals.

- The interval $(0,1)$ is not closed, so the extreme value theorem is not applicable.

- Now, consider $[0,2].$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0.5}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 0.5}(x-1)=(0.5)-1=-0.5, \\ {lim}_{x\to {0.5}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 0.5}(4-{x}^{2})=4-(0.5)^{2}=3.75.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits from the left and from the right of $x=0.5$ are not the same. Hence, $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=0.5.$ Therefore, $f(x)$ is not continuous on the interval $[0,2],$ and the extreme value theorem is not applicable on this interval.

- Finally, consider $[1,2].$ The only discontinuity of the function $f(x)$ is at $x=0.5,$ which is not in the interval $[1,2].$ Therefore, $f(x)$ is continuous on the interval $[1,2],$ and the extreme value theorem is applicable on this interval.

In conclusion, the correct answer is "III only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Convergence of a Power Series

:question/problem:
The power series ${\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }{a}_{n}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}^{n}$ converges at  $x=-1.$ Which of the following **must** be true?

- The series converges at $x=-\frac{3}{2}$
- The series diverges at $x=2$

The center of the expansion is $x=\frac{1}{2},$ and since the series is convergent for $x=-1,$ this means that the radius of convergence $R$ is *at least* $\frac{3}{2},$ i.e., $R\ge \frac{3}{2}.$ So, the series is convergent for every point in the interval $[-1,2).$ However, we know nothing about the convergence of the series at any point outside the interval $[-1,2).$

![](images/03/03901ede0b4fadb59556c63aa4534b3a9e20c1e8188388e6256434ece03d9211.png)

 

With this in mind, let's check each of our statements.

- Statement I is true. Since $0\in [-1,2),$ the series is convergent at $x=0.$

- Statement II is false. Since $-\frac{3}{2}\notin [-1,2),$ we cannot guarantee that the series is convergent at $x=-\frac{3}{2}.$

- Statement III is false. Since $2\notin [-1,2),$ we cannot guarantee that the series is divergent at $x=2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Invertible Affine Transformations

:question/problem:
Consider the affine transformation $T$ defined as

$$
x=u-v,\,y=u+2v+1.
$$

Suppose that $A$ is the matrix that represents the linear transformation associated with $T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]$
- $det(A)=0$
- The transformation is invertible
:question/worked-solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement I is false. The given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ u+2v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ u+2v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\ne [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- Statement II is false. Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|=1\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot 1=3\ne 0.
$$

- Statement III is true. Since $det(A)\ne 0,$ the affine transformation is invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

Let $A$ be the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]$
- $det(A)=-2$
- The transformation $T$ is orientation-preserving
:question/worked-solution:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement I is false. Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3u-v+2 \\ v-u\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3u-v \\ -u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].$

- Statement II is false. Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}|=3\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot (-1)=2.
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $det(A)>0,$ the affine transformation $T$ is orientation-preserving.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Determining a Flux's Sign From a Diagram

:question/problem:
![](images/77/772added7ce46ba0ec25de66dfd03e0107787d851006f261ac8843eba008a2d2.png)

Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. 

Which of the following statements are true?

- The flux of $F$ across $C$ is positive
- The flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero
- The flux of $F$ across $-C$ is negative
:question/worked-solution:
If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/a7/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero then the flux equals zero.

![](images/3a/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

For an arbitrary closed curve, the outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. From the diagram below we see that $F$ acts perpendicular to $n$ at every point on $C.$ Therefore, there is no net flow of $F$ through $C.$

![](images/d7/d7a469a331a3cda238fcefb9e7163743483975c4ecc7b962d6d5f8d79736693c.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](images/29/29f144d6f3ce8233a034025fe933bc57dbea5476c50a259853a98bd2a2b3a47b.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $-C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{-C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Determining Cases Where a Stream Function Exists

:question/problem:
Which of the following vector fields have a stream function?

- $F(x,y)=y\,i-x\,j$
- $F(x,y)=xy\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$
- $F(x,y)=2x\,i-y\,j$
:question/worked-solution:
A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each vector field.

- Vector field I has a stream function. Indeed, the partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=0,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0+0=0
$$

- Vector field II doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=y+2y\ne 0.
$$

- Vector field III doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2+(-1)\ne 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

- $f(x)$ is concave down on $(0,\infty )$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the second derivative of $f(x),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =2x-2{e}^{x} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2-2{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the function is concave up, we need to solve ${f}^{″}(x)>0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2-2{e}^{x} & >0 \\ {e}^{x} & <1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this inequality by considering the graph of $y={e}^{x}.$

![](images/c1/c199b110a3d19ecc23454f52dc7470af318ce871805595fd5fe7609dee5b0545.png)

From the graph, we see that ${e}^{x}<1$ when $x<0.$ So the graph is concave up on the interval $(-\infty ,0).$

The function $f(x)$ is concave down when ${f}^{″}(x)<0.$ By similar reasoning to before, this leads to the inequality ${e}^{x}>1,$ which has the solution $(0,\infty ).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

$$

To find where the function is concave up, we need to solve ${f}^{″}(x)>0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & >0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡x & >0.\end{aligned}

We can solve this inequality by considering the graph of $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ over the interval $(0,\pi ).$

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Singular Values of a Matrix

:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- Any $3\times 2$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
- The matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -1 & -5\end{aligned}]$ has one negative singular value.
- Any $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.
:question/worked-solution:
The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $2\times 2$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{2\times 3}\times {A}_{3\times 2}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{2\times 2}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $2$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is true. Since $A$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 2}\times {A}_{2\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

:question/problem:
Let $T:{R}^{5}\to {R}^{5}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T,$ and let ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ be a set of linearly independent vectors in ${R}^{5}.$ Consider the following statement:

*If  $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$, then $\text{__________}.$ *

Which of the following can be placed into the blank space to make a true statement?

- $\text{rank}(T)=1$
- $\text{nullity}(T)=2$
- $T$ is a bijection
:question/worked-solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{5}$ into ${R}^{5},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{5} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=5 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=5.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Since $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ and the set ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is linearly independent, we get that $\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=3.$

- Statement II is true. According to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =5-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =5-3 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $\text{rank}(T)\ne 5$ (or since $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0$), the linear transformation $T$ cannot be a bijection according to the invertible matrix theorem.

Therefore, the correct option is "II only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements Using the Rank-Nullity Theorem

:question/problem:
Let $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- If $\text{Im}(T)={[x,y,z]^{T}\,:\,3x+2y-z=0}$ then $\text{nullity}(T)=1$
- If ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are two different solutions to $Tx=[1,-2,1]^{T}$ then $T$ is invertible
- If ${v}_{1},$ ${v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}$ are the columns of $T$ and ${v}_{3}={v}_{1}+2{v}_{2}$, then $\text{Ker}(T)={0}$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{3}$ into ${R}^{3},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Solving $3x+2y-z=0$ for $z,$ we get $z=3x+2y.$ Therefore, any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ 3x+2y\end{aligned}]=x{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+y{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(T)=2.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are two different solutions to $Tx=[1,-2,1]^{T},$ then 

$$
T{v}_{1}=T{v}_{2}\,⟹\,T({v}_{1}-{v}_{2})=0,
$$

where ${v}_{1}-{v}_{2}$ is a non-zero vector. This means that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Null}(T)\ne {0}$ and, according to the invertible matrix theorem, $T$ can't be invertible.

- Statement III is false. If the columns of $T$ are such that ${v}_{3}={v}_{1}+2{v}_{2},$ then the set of vectors ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is linearly dependent and therefore $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T)\ne {R}^{3}.$ Now, according to the matrix invertible theorem, we obtain that $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Open and Closed Sets in the Plane in Set Notation

:question/problem:
Which of the following sets are closed?

- ${(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,0\le y\le x+1,\,-1\le x\le 1}$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that:

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Let's examine our sets in turn.

- The first set is *closed* since it contains all of its boundary points (all the corresponding inequalities are not strict).

- The second set is *open* since it doesn't contain any of its boundary points (all the corresponding inequalities are strict).

- The third set is *closed* since it contains all of its boundary points (all the corresponding inequalities are not strict).

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Checking Whether a Given Function Is a Valid PDF

:question/problem:
$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{1-x},\, & x\ge 1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Given the function $f(x)$ above, which of the following statements are true?

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\ge 1$
- ${\int }_{1}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$
- $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function
:question/worked-solution:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for $x\ge 1$, we have $f(x)={e}^{1-x}\ge 0.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }{e}^{1-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-{e}^{1-x}]}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =0-(-{e}^{0}) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Since statements I and II are true, the first and second conditions are satisfied. So, $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Image of a Horizontal Segment Under a Polar Transformation

:question/problem:
![](images/b8/b8874b14fa80881e69cb1daee180d2e342a27c5902e66fc75d43622278176b09.png)

Consider the square region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le \sqrt{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{6}\le v\le \frac{\pi }{3}},
$$

and the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:(u,v)\to (u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v).
$$

The image of the bottom side of $Δ$ under the action of $T$ is a line segment. Which of the following statements are true regarding the image?

- The image makes the angle of $\frac{\pi }{6}$ with the positive $x$-axis.
- The image makes the angle of $\frac{\pi }{3}$ with the positive $x$-axis.
- The endpoints of the image lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $2$ centered at $O.$
:question/worked-solution:
To map the entire region $Δ$ onto the $xy$-plane, we consider the transformation of each side. However, in this case, we consider only the bottom side.

For the bottom side, we have $v=\frac{\pi }{6}$ and $1\le u\le \sqrt{2}.$ 

Substituting $v=\frac{\pi }{6}$ into our transformation equations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x,y) & =T(u,v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v) \\  & =(u\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}),\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})),\,\frac{\pi }{6}\le v\le \frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a parametric equation of the line segment shown below.

![](images/fc/fcfc165548d8174ec0468dce53317fd0c8daa14565852c5e44d6764161723bed.png)

 

Note that the line that this segment lies on passes through the origin. 

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. The slope of the line is

$$
k=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})}=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}).
$$

As a result, our line makes an angle of $\frac{\pi }{6}$ radians with the positive $x$-axis.

- Statement III is false.

- When $u=1,$ we obtain the point 
$(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})),$
whose distance to the origin is $1.$

- When $u=\sqrt{2},$ we obtain the point 
$(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}),\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})),$
whose distance to the origin is $\sqrt{2}.$

So, the endpoints of the line segment lie on the circles of radii $1$ and $\sqrt{2}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Inverse Function Theorem

:question/problem:
Let $f:U\to R$ be continuously differentiable on an open set $U⊆R$ such that $f(a)=b$ and ${f}^{′}(a)\ne 0$ for $a\in U.$ Which of the following statements **must** be true?

- The function $f$ is invertible on $U.$
- The inverse ${f}^{-1}$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $b.$
- The derivative of ${f}^{-1}$ is given by ${({f}^{-1})}^{′}(b)=-{f}^{′}(a).$
:question/worked-solution:
The inverse function theorem for single-variable functions states the following:

*If $f:U\to R$ is continuously differentiable on an open set $U⊆R,$ $f(a)=b$ and ${f}^{′}(a)\ne 0$ for $a\in U,$ then*

- *$f$ is invertible in some neighborhood of $a,$*

- *${f}^{-1},$ the inverse of $f,$ is continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $b,$ and*

- *the derivative of ${f}^{-1}$ is given by* 

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(b)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(a)}=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(b))}\,.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. According to the theorem, the function $f$ must be invertible in some neighborhood of $a,$ which could be smaller than $U.$ 

For example, the function $f(x)={x}^{2}$ satisfies the conditions of the inverse function theorem for $U=(-2,2)$ and $a=1.$ However, $f(x)$ is not invertible on the entire set $U,$ only on a subset of $U.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the inverse ${f}^{-1}$ must be continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of $b.$

- Statement III is false. According to the theorem, we must have ${({f}^{-1})}^{′}(b)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(a)}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: None of the statements are true.

:question/problem:
$$
{u}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$
- ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthogonal
- ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthonormal
:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]=18-18=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. Notice that, for example, $Q({u}_{1})$ is not a unit vector since

$$
‖Q({u}_{1})‖=‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{{9}^{2}+{6}^{2}}\ne 1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

- ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthonormal
:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=0.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Sets Defined Using Inequalities

:question/problem:
Which of the following sets are infinite?

I. $A={n\in Z\,:\,{n}^{2}-5n+6>0}$

II. $B={m\in Z\,:\,{m}^{2}-5m+6<0}$

III. $C={q\in Q\,:\,{q}^{2}-5q+6<0}$
:question/worked-solution:
The cardinality of a finite set is the number of elements contained within it. A set is infinite if it has infinitely many elements. 

Let's start by analyzing the parabola $y={x}^{2}-5x+6$ for $x\in R.$

First, we find the roots of the parabola:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-5x+6 & =0 \\ (x-2)(x-3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the roots are $x=2$ and $x=3,$ and we can graph the parabola as follows:

![](images/0a/0a42815f626652c332862a38a3812463a9407605329bd81df25f11274b26ce6f.png)

Therefore:

- The solution to the inequality ${x}^{2}-5x+6>0$ for $x\in R$ is 

$$
x<2\,\text{or}\,x>3
$$

and can be expressed as $x\in {I}_{1}=(-\infty ,2)\cup (3,\infty ).$

- Similarly, the solution to the inequality ${x}^{2}-5x+6<0$ for $x\in R$ is 

$$
2<x<3
$$

and can be expressed as $x\in {I}_{2}=(2,3).$

With these in mind, let's examine our sets:

- The set $A$ is infinite. If $n\in Z,$ the solutions to the inequality ${n}^{2}-5n+6>0$ are all the integers that lie in the interval ${I}_{1}.$ Therefore,

$$
A={…,0,1}\cup {4,5,…}.
$$

- The set $B$ is finite. If $m\in Z,$ the solutions to the inequality ${m}^{2}-5m+6<0$ are all the integers that lie in the interval ${I}_{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
B={}.
$$

Consequently, $|B|=0,$ which is finite.

- The set $C$ is infinite. If $q\in Q,$ the solutions to ${q}^{2}-5q+6<0$ are all the rational numbers that lie in the interval ${I}_{2}.$ Since any real interval of nonzero length contains infinitely many rational numbers, it follows that $C$ is infinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$A$ and $C$ only."

Which of the following sets are infinite?

- $A={n\in Z\,:\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2n\pi )=1}$
- $B={q\in Q\,:\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2q\pi )=1}$
- $C={x\in R\,:\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\pi )=1}$
:question/worked-solution:
The cardinality of a finite set is the number of elements contained within it. A set is infinite if it has infinitely many elements. 

We start by finding the solutions to the equation $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\pi )=1$ for $x\in R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x\pi  & =\frac{\pi }{2}+2m\pi  \\ x & =\frac{1}{4}+m,\,m\in Z\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets:

- The set $A$ is finite. There are no values of $m\in Z$ such that $\frac{1}{4}+m\in Z.$ Therefore,

$$
A={}.
$$

Consequently, $|A|=0,$ which is finite.

- The set $B$ is infinite. Listing the elements of $B$ for different values of $m,$ we have

$$
B={…,-\frac{3}{4},\frac{1}{4},\frac{5}{4},\frac{9}{4},…}.
$$

- The set $C$ is infinite. Since $B$ is infinite, and $B⊆C,$ it follows that $C$ is infinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$B$ and $C$ only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Sets Defined Using Derivatives

:question/problem:
Which of the following sets are infinite?

- $A={{f}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}({x}^{2})\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}}$
- $B={{g}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}}$
- $C={{h}^{(n)}(x)=\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}(\sqrt{x})\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}}$
:question/worked-solution:
The cardinality of a finite set is the number of elements contained within it. A set is infinite if it has infinitely many elements. 

- The set $A$ is finite. Listing a few elements of our set, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{(0)}(x) & ={x}^{2} \\ {f}^{(1)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})=2x \\ {f}^{(2)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)=2 \\ {f}^{(3)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2)=0 \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(0)=0 \\  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, for $n>3,$ we have ${f}^{(n)}(x)=0.$ Listing a few elements of our set, we have the following:

$$
A={{x}^{2},2x,2,0}.
$$

Consequently, $|A|=4,$ which is finite.

- The set $B$ is finite. Listing the first few elements of our set, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{(0)}(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x=\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ {g}^{(1)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=\frac{1}{x} \\ {g}^{(2)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x})=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ {g}^{(3)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})=\frac{2}{{x}^{3}} \\ ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we can write our set as follows:

$$
B={\operatorname{ln}⁡x,\frac{1}{x},-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}},…}
$$

Consequently, $B$ is infinite.

- The set $C$ is infinite. Similar to the previous case, listing the first few elements of our set, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{(0)}(x) & =\sqrt{x} \\ {h}^{(1)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ {h}^{(2)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}})=-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{x}^{3}}} \\ {h}^{(3)}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{x}^{3}}})=\frac{3}{8\sqrt{{x}^{5}}} \\ ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we can write our set as follows:

$$
C={\sqrt{x},\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}},-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{{x}^{3}}},\frac{3}{8\sqrt{{x}^{5}}},…}
$$

Consequently, $C$ is infinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$B$ and $C$ only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Sets Defined Using Inequalities

:question/problem:
Which of the following sets are infinite?

I. $A={n\in Z\,:\,|2n|>5}$

II. $B={q\in Q\,:\,|2q|>5}$

III. $C={x\in R\,:\,|2x|>5}$
:question/worked-solution:
The cardinality of a finite set is the number of elements contained within it. A set is infinite if it has infinitely many elements. 

We start by solving the following inequality for $x\in R:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x|>5 \\ 2|x|>5 \\ |x|>\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
x<-\frac{5}{2}\,\text{or}\,x>\frac{5}{2}
$$

and can be expressed as $x\in I=(-\infty ,-\frac{5}{2})\cup (\frac{5}{2},\infty ).$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our sets:

- The set $A$ is infinite. If $n\in Z,$ the solutions to the inequality $|2n|>5$ are all the integers that lie in the interval $I.$ Therefore, 

$$
A={…,-4,-3}\cup {3,4,…}.
$$

- The set $B$ is infinite. If $q\in Q,$ the solutions to $|2q|>5$ are all the rational numbers that lie in the interval $I.$ Since any real interval of nonzero length contains infinitely many rational numbers, it follows that $B$ is infinite.

- The set $C$ is infinite. Since $B$ is infinite, and $B⊂C,$ it follows that $C$ is infinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$A,B,$ and $C.$"

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Divisibility of a Product

:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. If $15\,|\,32b$ then $15\,|\,b$

II. If ${7}^{2}\,|\,7b$ then ${7}^{2}\,|\,b$

III. If ${3}^{2}\,|\,25b$ then $9\,|\,b$
:question/worked-solution:
For any integers $a,$ $b,$ and $c,$

$c\,|\,ab\,$ and $\,\text{gcd}(a,c)=1$ $\,⟹\,$ $\,c\,|\,b.$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements.

- Statement I is true. First, note that $\text{gcd}(15,32)=1.$ Therefore, we have $15\,|\,32b$ and $\text{gcd}(15,32)=1,$ which implies $15\,|\,b.$

- Statement II is false. As a counterexample, let $b=7.$ Then, ${7}^{2}∣7\cdot 7$ but ${7}^{2}∤7.$

- Statement III is true. First, note that $\text{gcd}({3}^{2},25)=1.$ Therefore, we have ${3}^{2}∣25b$ and $\text{gcd}({3}^{2},25)=1,$ which implies ${3}^{2}\,|\,b.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Representing Binary Relations Using Graphs

:question/problem:
![](images/01/015cb5b350ad2692c1371d20c367e6c01a81b981351ba33b61e6c95854862d63.png)

The plot of the binary relation $S,$ defined over the sets $X={2,3,4}$ and $Y={♣,♠},$ is given above. Which of the following ordered pairs belong to the relation?

I. $(2,♠)$

II. $(3,♣)$

III. $(4,♣)$
:question/worked-solution:
A binary relation can be visualized using a plot (or graph), where 

- the first set is plotted along the horizontal axis,

- the second set is plotted along the vertical axis, and

- each pair $(x,y)$ from the relation defines a point with coordinates $(x,y)$ on the plot.

With that in mind, let's examine the given ordered pairs.

- The pair $(2,♠)$ belongs to the relation. Indeed, the plot contains a point with these coordinates.

- The pair $(3,♣)$ does not belong to the relation since the plot does not contain a point with such coordinates.

- The pair $(4,♣)$ belongs to the relation. Indeed, the plot contains a point with these coordinates.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Representing Binary Relations Using Digraphs

:question/problem:
![](images/84/847bcee3b9f9fc6672d5858111866141e043e390605cd92fb5579fd5193d7df4.png)

The directed graph of a relation defined on the set ${1,2,3}$ is given above. Which of the following ordered pairs belong to the relation?

I. $(2,1)$

II. $(3,3)$

III. $(2,3)$
:question/worked-solution:
A binary relation can be visualized using a directed graph (digraph), where 

- the nodes (vertices) of the graph are elements of the underlying set,

- each pair $(x,y)$ from the relation defines an arrow from node $x$ to node $y$,

- each pair $(x,x)$ from the relation defines a loop from node $x$ to itself.

With that in mind, let's examine the given ordered pairs.

- The pair $(2,1)$ belongs to the relation. Indeed, the directed graph has an arrow that starts at the node $2$ and ends at the node $1.$

- The pair $(3,3)$ belongs to the relation. Indeed, the directed graph has a loop from the node $3$ to itself.

- The pair $(2,3)$ does not belong to the relation since the directed graph does not have an arrow that starts at the node $2$ and ends at the node $3.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Symmetric and Antisymmetric Relations From a Diagram

:question/problem:
![](images/fd/fdbcfe164fcca0e005255de10f10c10bedc156f3a582eeb5800322d4c4ebe0ab.png)

Which of the plots above represent symmetric relations defined on the set $A={0,2,4}?$
:question/worked-solution:
First, recall the following definitions:

- A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is *symmetric* if for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,⟹\,(y,x)\in R.
$$

In terms of a plot, if a point $(x,y)$ belongs to the plot, then $(y,x),$ the point symmetric to $(x,y)$ over the diagonal line $y=x,$ should also be on the plot.

- A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is *antisymmetric* if for all $x,y\in A,$ we have

$$
(x,y)\in R\,\text{and}\,(y,x)\in R\,⟹\,x=y.
$$

So, only one of the points, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be on the plot of an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows points on the diagonal line $y=x.$

With that in mind, let's draw the diagonal line $y=x$ and examine our plots.

![](images/9c/9c9c16300cfb95a61a261e39db865d5c6d056794bd7aaa422567bde10dd4abf5.png)

 

- Plot I represents a symmetric relation since the plot is symmetric over the line $y=x.$

- Plot II represents an antisymmetric relation since the plot contains at most one point from each pair of the points symmetric over the line $y=x.$

- Plot III represents neither a symmetric nor an antisymmetric relation. It's not symmetric since, for example, the pair $(4,2)$ belongs to the plot while the point $(2,4)$ does not. And it's not antisymmetric since it contains the pairs $(0,4)$ and $(4,0).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
