Thus, equation III is exact.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Checking ODEs for Exactness

:question/problem:
Which of the following differential equations is exact?  

- $(2xy+5)\,\text{d}x+({x}^{2}+7)\,\text{d}y=0$
- $({y}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}x+(xy+1)\,\text{d}y=0$
- $(5y-3x)\,\text{d}y-(y-2x)\,\text{d}x=0$
:question/worked-solution:
A differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\text{d}y=0
$$

is exact if it passes the exactness test, i.e.,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}.
$$

Now, let's consider each equation:

- The first equation is

$$
(2xy+5)\,\text{d}x+({x}^{2}+7)\,\text{d}y=0.
$$

 
Therefore, the functions $P$ and $Q$ are

$$
P(x,y)=2xy+5,\,Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+7.
$$

Now, let's compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+5) \\  & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+7) \\  & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}.\,✓
$$

 
Thus, equation I is exact.

- The second equation is

$$
({y}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}x+(xy+1)\,\text{d}y=0.
$$

Therefore, the functions $P$ and $Q$ are

$$
P(x,y)={y}^{2}+x,\,Q(x,y)=xy+1.
$$

Now, let's compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+x) \\  & =2y\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+1) \\  & =y\end{aligned}
$$

So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}\ne \frac{∂Q}{∂x}.\,\times 
$$

Thus, equation II is not exact.

- The third equation is

$$
(5y-3x)\,\text{d}y-(y-2x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Therefore, the functions $P$ and $Q$ are

$$
P(x,y)=-(y-2x)=2x-y,\,Q(x,y)=5y-3x.
$$

Now, let's compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x-y) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5y-3x) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

 
So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}\ne \frac{∂Q}{∂x}.\,\times 
$$

Thus, equation III is not exact.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying a True Statement Concerning a 2x2 System of Equations

:question/problem:
Consider a system of two linear equations in two variables, represented by the matrix equation $Ax=b$ in the usual way. Given that the system has exactly one solution, which of the following statements are true?

- $A$ is invertible
- $det(A)=0$
- $Ax=0$ has an infinite number of solutions
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

Also, we are told that the second part of the invertible matrix theorem is true. So, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement I is true by the first part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement II is false by the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement III is false by the third part of the invertible matrix theorem.

Therefore, only statement I is true.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying an Elementary 2x2 Matrix

:question/problem:
Which of the following are elementary matrices?

$$
W=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ \frac{3}{4} & 1\end{aligned}],\,Y=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4} & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,Z=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
:question/worked-solution:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation. 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- The matrix $W$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{3}{4}{R}_{1},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{3}{4}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ \frac{3}{4} & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =W\end{aligned}
$$

- The matrix $Y$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

- The matrix $Z$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =Z\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only $W$ and $Z$ are elementary matrices.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Applying the Linearity Principle to the Solutions of a Homogeneous System of ODEs

:question/problem:
Suppose ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are both solutions of the homogeneous system
${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t).$
Which of the following is **always** a solution of the same system?

- $x(t)=2\cdot {x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t)$
- $x(t)={x}_{1}(t)-t\cdot {x}_{2}(t)$
- $x(t)={x}_{1}(t)⊙{x}_{2}(t)$ (element-wise product)
:question/worked-solution:
The *linearity principle* for systems of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) states that if ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are solutions to a homogeneous linear system, then for any constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2},$ the linear combination 

$$
{c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)
$$

is also a solution of the system. 

With that in mind, let's examine the given expressions.

- Option I is a solution to the system. Indeed, notice that

$$
2\cdot {x}_{1}(t)+(-1)\cdot {x}_{2}(t)
$$

is a linear combination of the solutions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ with constant multiplies ${c}_{1}=2$ and ${c}_{2}=-1,$ respectively.

- Option II might be *not* a solution to the system since it's not a linear combination of the solutions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ Notice that the multiplier of the second term is not a constant.

- Option III might be *not* a solution to the system since it's not a linear combination of the solutions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Block Diagonal and Block Triangular Matrices

:question/problem:
Which of the following matrices are block diagonal?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 7 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$
:question/worked-solution:
A block diagonal matrix can be partitioned so that it has only square blocks on the main diagonal, and all the other blocks contain only zeros.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- $A$ is *not* a block diagonal matrix since it can't be partitioned in the way described above:

$$
\begin{aligned}A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- $B$ is *not* a block diagonal matrix since it can't be partitioned in the way described above:

$$
\begin{aligned}B=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- $C$ is a block diagonal matrix. Indeed, we can partition it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}C=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 7 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$C$ only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Block Diagonal and Block Triangular Matrices

:question/problem:
Which of the following matrices are block lower triangular?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & 0 \\ -6 & 4 & 10\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$
:question/worked-solution:
A block lower triangular matrix can be partitioned so that it has only square blocks on the main diagonal, and the blocks above the main diagonal contain only zeros.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- $A$ is a block lower triangular matrix. Indeed, we can partition it as follows:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & 0 \\ -6 & 4 & 10\end{aligned}]
$$

- $B$ is *not* a block lower triangular matrix since it can't be partitioned in the way described above:

$$
\begin{aligned}B=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- $C$ is a block lower triangular matrix. Indeed, we can partition it as follows:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$A$ and $C$ only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying the Runge-Kutta Method

:question/problem:
Consider the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(0)=1
$$

for some function $f(x,y).$ The table below shows the intermediate quantities computed in the first iteration of the Runge-Kutta (RK4) method.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $4$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  |

Given that the step size is $Δx=\frac{1}{4},$ at which of the following points is the function $f$ evaluated during this iteration?

- $(\frac{1}{8},\frac{3}{2})$
- $(\frac{1}{8},\frac{3}{4})$
- $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{5}{8})$
:question/worked-solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c
$$

the increment in $y$ using the Runge-Kutta (RK4) method with step size $Δx$ is computed as the weighted average of four sample slopes:

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the initial point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{1}^{′}=f({x}_{1},{y}_{1})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{2}^{′}=f({x}_{2},{y}_{2})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{3}^{′}=f({x}_{3},{y}_{3})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{3},{y}_{3})=(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx).$

Now, we have the following table of values:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $4$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ |  |

With this in mind, let's find each point at which the slope is evaluated in turn using the values given in the table.

- The slope ${y}^{′}$ is evaluated at the initial point $(x,y)=({x}_{0},{y}_{0})=(0,1).$

- The estimated slope ${y}_{1}^{′}$ is evaluated at

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{1},{y}_{1}) & =(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(0+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4},\,1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot \frac{1}{4}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{8},\frac{3}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

- The estimated slope ${y}_{2}^{′}$ is evaluated at

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{2},{y}_{2}) & =(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(0+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4},\,1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-2)\cdot \frac{1}{4}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{8},\frac{3}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

- The estimated slope ${y}_{3}^{′}$ is evaluated at

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{3},{y}_{3}) & =(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(0+\frac{1}{4},\,1+(-1)\cdot \frac{1}{4}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, of the given options, the slope is evaluated at the points "I and II only".

Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ satisfy the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t)$ and ${x}_{p}(t)$ satisfy the inhomogeneous system
${x}^{′}(t)=A\text{ }x(t)+f(t).$
Which of the following is **always** a solution of the same inhomogeneous system?

- $2\cdot {x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$
- $-5\cdot {x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{p}(t)$
- $3\cdot {x}_{1}(t)-2\cdot {x}_{2}(t)+3\cdot {x}_{p}(t)$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that if ${x}_{h}(t)$ satisfies a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution to an inhomogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t),$ then ${x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)$ is also a solution to the same inhomogeneous system.

Additonally, the *linearity principle* for systems of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) states that if ${x}_{1}(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t),…,{x}_{k}(t)$ are solutions to a homogeneous linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ then any linear combination 

$$
{c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)+⋯+{c}_{k}{x}_{k}(t)
$$

with ${c}_{1},{c}_{2},…,{c}_{k}\in R$ is also a solution of the same homogeneous system. 

With that in mind, let's examine the given expression.

- Option I is a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Indeed, notice that the linear combination 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)=2\cdot {x}_{1}(t)+1\cdot {x}_{2}(t)
$$

is a solution to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ according to the linearity principle. Thus, 

$$
{{2\cdot {x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{h}(t)}+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

is a solution to our inhomogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t).$

- Option II might be *not* a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that $-5\cdot {x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{p}(t)$ can't be written as 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),
$$

where ${x}_{h}(t)$ is a solution of the homogeneous system, because of the multiplier $-1$ next to the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$

- Option III might be *not* a solution to the inhomogeneous system. Notice that $3\cdot {x}_{1}(t)-2\cdot {x}_{2}(t)+3\cdot {x}_{p}(t)$ can't be written as 

$$
{x}_{h}(t)+{x}_{p}(t),
$$

where ${x}_{h}(t)$ is a solution of the homogeneous system, because of the multiplier $3$ next to the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying the Runge-Kutta Method

:question/problem:
Consider the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(1)=2
$$

for some function $f(x,y).$ The table below shows the intermediate quantities computed in the first iteration of the Runge-Kutta (RK4) method.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $2$ | $-2$ | $0$ | $3$ |  |

Given that the step size is $Δx=\frac{1}{2},$ at which of the following points is the function $f$ evaluated during this iteration?

- $(\frac{5}{4},\frac{5}{2})$
- $(\frac{5}{4},\frac{3}{2})$
- $(\frac{3}{2},2)$
:question/worked-solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c
$$

the increment in $y$ using the Runge-Kutta (RK4) method with step size $Δx$ is computed as the weighted average of four sample slopes:

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{6}({y}^{′}+2{y}_{1}^{′}+2{y}_{2}^{′}+{y}_{3}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the initial point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{1}^{′}=f({x}_{1},{y}_{1})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{2}^{′}=f({x}_{2},{y}_{2})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{2},{y}_{2})=(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx),$

- ${y}_{3}^{′}=f({x}_{3},{y}_{3})$ is the estimated slope at $({x}_{3},{y}_{3})=(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx).$

Now, we have the following table of values:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{1}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{2}^{′}\,$ | $\,{y}_{3}^{′}\,$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $2$ | $2$ | $-2$ | $0$ | $3$ |  |

With this in mind, let's find each point at which the slope is evaluated in turn using the values given in the table.

- The slope ${y}^{′}$ is evaluated at the initial point $(x,y)=({x}_{0},{y}_{0})=(1,2).$

- The estimated slope ${y}_{1}^{′}$ is evaluated at

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{1},{y}_{1}) & =(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2},\,2+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{5}{4},\frac{5}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

- The estimated slope ${y}_{2}^{′}$ is evaluated at

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{2},{y}_{2}) & =(x+\frac{1}{2}Δx,\,y+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{1}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2},\,2+\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-2)\cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{5}{4},\frac{3}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

- The estimated slope ${y}_{3}^{′}$ is evaluated at

$$
\begin{aligned}({x}_{3},{y}_{3}) & =(x+Δx,\,y+{y}_{2}^{′}\cdot Δx) \\  & =(1+\frac{1}{2},\,2+0\cdot \frac{1}{2}) \\  & =(\frac{3}{2},2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, of the given options, the slope is evaluated at the points "I, II, and III".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying a Decoupled System of Linear ODEs

:question/problem:
Which of the following systems of linear ODEs are decoupled?

- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=6{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=4{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}$
- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=5{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-8{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}$
- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}$
:question/worked-solution:
A *decoupled system* consists of equations depending on only one variable, such as

$$
{x}_{i}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{i}{x}_{i}(t),
$$

where ${\lambda }_{i}$ is a constant. This means that we can solve each equation independently. 

With this in mind, let's examine our systems.

- System I is *not* decoupled because some of its equations depend on more than one variable. For example, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=6{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$

- System II is decoupled since its equations depend on only one variable each. Indeed, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=5{x}_{1}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-8{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{2}(t).$

- System III is *not* decoupled because some of its equations depend on more than one variable. For example, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Homogeneous and Inhomogeneous ODEs

:question/problem:
Which of the following first-order linear differential equations are inhomogeneous?

- ${y}^{′}+{x}^{2}y=3x$
- ${y}^{′}+{x}^{2}y=0$
- ${y}^{′}+{x}^{2}y=y$
:question/worked-solution:
A first-order linear differential equation is homogeneous if it can be written in the form

$$
{y}^{′}+P(x)y=0.
$$

A first-order linear differential equation is inhomogeneous if it is not homogeneous, i.e., if it can be written as

$$
{y}^{′}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

where $Q$ is not identical to zero.

To determine which equations are inhomogeneous, we examine each one in turn.

- First, we consider the equation

$$
{y}^{′}+{x}^{2}y=3x.
$$

Notice that this is written in the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=Q(x)$ where $Q(x)=3x$ is not identically zero. Therefore, this equation is inhomogeneous.

- Next, we consider the equation

$$
{y}^{′}+{x}^{2}y=0.
$$

Notice that this equation has the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=0.$ Therefore, this equation is homogeneous.

- Finally, we consider the equation

$$
{y}^{′}+{x}^{2}y=y.
$$

We collect the $y$-terms on the left side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}+{x}^{2}y & =y \\ {y}^{′}+{x}^{2}y-y & =0 \\ {y}^{′}+({x}^{2}-1)y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since our equation can be written in the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=0,$ the equation is homogeneous.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Homogeneous and Inhomogeneous ODEs

:question/problem:
Which of the following first-order linear differential equations are homogeneous?

- ${y}^{′}+2{x}^{3}y={x}^{2}$
- ${y}^{′}+2{x}^{3}y=-3y$
- ${y}^{′}+2{x}^{3}y=0$
:question/worked-solution:
A first-order linear differential equation is homogeneous if it can be written in the form

$$
{y}^{′}+P(x)y=0.
$$

Now, let's consider each equation in turn.

- First, we consider the equation

$$
{y}^{′}+2{x}^{3}y={x}^{2}.
$$

Notice that this is written in the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=Q(x)$ where $Q(x)={x}^{2}$ is not identically zero. Therefore, this equation is inhomogeneous.

- Next, we consider the equation

$$
{y}^{′}+2{x}^{3}y=-3y.
$$

We move the term involving $y$ to the left side so that all $y$-terms are together:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}+2{x}^{3}y & =-3y \\ {y}^{′}+2{x}^{3}y+3y & =0 \\ {y}^{′}+(2{x}^{3}+3)y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This matches the homogeneous form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=0.$  Therefore, this equation *is* homogeneous.

- Finally, we consider the equation

$$
{y}^{′}+2{x}^{3}y=0.
$$

The right-hand side is already zero, so the equation directly matches the form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=0.$ Therefore, this equation is homogeneous.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

$$

This matches the homogeneous form ${y}^{′}+P(x)y=0.$  Therefore, this equation *is* homogeneous.

Which of the following systems of linear ODEs are decoupled?

:question/worked-solution:

$$

$$

- System III is decoupled since its equations depend on only one variable each. Indeed, ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-9{x}_{1}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=6{x}_{2}(t)$ depends on only ${x}_{2}(t).$

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Proving the Smoothness Property

:question/problem:
Let $f(t)$ be a piecewise function defined on $[0,\infty )$ with exponential order $a,$ and consider its Laplace transform 

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)},\,s>a.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- If $f(t)$ contains a discontinuity for some value of $t>0,$ we have $F(s)=0$ for all $s>a.$
- $F(s)$ is infinitely differentiable on $s>a.$
- The Laplace transform converts a non-smooth $f(t)$ into a smooth function of $s.$
:question/worked-solution:
If a function $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty )$ and has exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}
$$

exists for every real $s>a,$ and $F$ is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence. 

The smoothness property states that, for each integer $n\ge 0$ and $s>a,$ we have

$$
{F}^{(n)}(s)=(-1)^{n}\,L{{t}^{n}f(t)}.
$$

Let's consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Smoothness has no bearing on whether the Laplace transform vanishes.
A function of exponential order always has a well-defined Laplace transform for $s>a$, and there is no reason for that transform to be identically zero.

- Statement II is true. The smoothness theorem states that for $f(t)$ of exponential order, the Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=L{f}(s)
$$

is infinitely differentiable at every point in its region of convergence, and we have

$$
{F}^{(n)}(s)=(-1)^{n}\,L{{t}^{n}f(t)}(s).
$$

- Statement III is true. The Laplace transform $F(s)$ of a function $f(t)$ is always infinitely differentiable in its region of convergence, even if $f(t)$ is non-smooth.

Therefore, the answer is "II and III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Determining Stability in Euler's Method

:question/problem:
For which of the following values is Euler's method stable, given that $\lambda $ is the parameter of the test equation ${y}^{′}=-\lambda y$ with $y=y(x),y(0)=1,x\ge 0,\lambda >0,$ and step size $Δx?$  

- $\lambda Δx=0.4$
- $\lambda Δx=2.0$
- $\lambda Δx=2.4$
- $\lambda Δx=1.2$

*Hint: The stability function for Euler's method is given by* $R(\lambda Δx)=1-\lambda Δx.$
:question/worked-solution:
A numerical method
${y}_{n+1}={y}_{n}+Δ{y}_{n}$
is stable for a given step size $Δx$ if, when applied to the test equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-\lambda y,\,y(0)=1,\,x\ge 0,\,\lambda >0,
$$

the numerical solution satisfies ${y}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty ,$ just like the exact solution.

For stability, we require that the following condition holds:

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(\lambda Δx)| & <1 \\ |1-\lambda Δx| & <1\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this gives

$$
0<\lambda Δx<2.
$$

This means that Euler's method is stable when applied to the test equation for values in the region $0<\lambda Δx<2.$ Of the given values:

- $\lambda Δx=0.4$ falls *within* the given region,

- $\lambda Δx=2.0$ falls *outside* of the given region,

- $\lambda Δx=2.4$ falls *outside* the given region, and

- $\lambda Δx=1.2$ falls *within* the given region.

Hence, Euler's method is stable for $\lambda Δx=0.4$ and $\lambda Δx=1.2$ only.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and IV only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements About the Stability of Euler's Method

:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true when testing the stability of Euler's method on the test equation ${y}^{′}=-\lambda y$ with $y=y(x),\,y(0)=3,\,x\ge 0,\,\lambda =\frac{7}{3},$ and step size $Δx?$  

- The update formula can be written as ${y}_{n+1}={(1-\frac{7}{3}Δx)}^{n}{y}_{n}.$
- The method is stable for $|1-\frac{7}{3}Δx|>1.$
- The method is stable for step size $Δx=0.2.$
- The method is **unstable** for step size $Δx=0.9.$
:question/worked-solution:
A numerical method ${y}_{n+1}={y}_{n}+Δ{y}_{n}$ is stable for a given step size $Δx$ if, when applied to the test equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-\lambda y,\,y(0)=3,\,x\ge 0,\,\lambda >0,
$$

the numerical solution satisfies ${y}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty ,$ just like the exact solution.

Now, let's check the stability of Euler's Method by applying it to the test equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-\frac{7}{3}y,\,y(0)=3.
$$

First, for an initial value problem ${y}^{′}=f(x,y),y({x}_{0})={y}_{0},$ Euler's method is given by the update formula

$$
{y}_{n+1}={y}_{n}+f({x}_{n},{y}_{n})\cdot Δx.
$$

Now, let's check our statements:

- Applying Euler's method to the test equation, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{n+1} & ={y}_{n}+(-\frac{7}{3}{y}_{n})\cdot Δx \\  & ={y}_{n}-\frac{7}{3}{y}_{n}\cdot Δx \\  & =(1-\frac{7}{3}Δx){y}_{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, statement I is false.

- For stability, we require ${y}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ Here, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{n} & =(1-\frac{7}{3}Δx){y}_{n-1} \\  & =(1-\frac{7}{3}Δx)((1-\frac{7}{3}Δx){y}_{n-2}) \\  & ={(1-\frac{7}{3}Δx)}^{2}{y}_{n-2} \\  & \,\,⋮\,\,⋮ \\  & ={(1-\frac{7}{3}Δx)}^{n}{y}_{0} \\  & =3{(1-\frac{7}{3}Δx)}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${y}_{n}$ converges to $0$ as $n\to \infty $ if and only if $|1-\frac{7}{3}Δx|<1,$ as stated. Hence, statement II is false.

- Expanding the inequality $|1-\frac{7}{3}Δx|<1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & <1-\frac{7}{3}Δx<1 \\ -2 & <-\frac{7}{3}Δx<0 \\ 0 & <\frac{7}{3}Δx<2 \\ 0 & <Δx<\frac{6}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine stability for the given step sizes:

- Since $Δx=0.2$ satisfies the above inequality, Euler's method is stable for this value. Hence, statement III is true.

- Since $Δx=0.9$ does not satisfy the above inequality, Euler's method is unstable for this value. Hence, statement IV is true.

In conclusion, the correct answer is "III and IV only".

- the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0,
$$

- the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0,
$$

then the method is of order $p.$

With that in mind, let's check each option in turn:

- For the LTE expression $τ(Δx)=2(Δx)^{2},$ the dominant term as $Δx\to 0$ is $2(Δx)^{2}=2(Δx)^{1+1}.$ So, statement I corresponds to an order $1$ method.

- For the GTE expression $e(Δx)=3(Δx)^{3}-3(Δx)^{2},$ the dominant term as $Δx\to 0$ is $-3(Δx)^{2}.$ So, statement II corresponds to an order $2$ method.

- For the LTE expression $τ(Δx)=(Δx)^{4}-2(Δx)^{5},$ the dominant term as $Δx\to 0$ is $(Δx)^{4}=(Δx)^{3+1}.$ So, statement III corresponds to an order $3$ method.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

$$

the numerical solution satisfies ${y}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty ,$ just like the exact solution.

$$

$$

:question/problem:
For which of the following step sizes is Euler's Method **stable**, given that $\lambda $ is the parameter of the test equation ${y}^{′}=-\lambda y$ with $y=y(x),y(0)=1,x\ge 0,\lambda >0,$ and step size $Δx?$

- $Δx=\frac{0.25}{\lambda }$
- $Δx=\frac{3.5}{\lambda }$
- $Δx=\frac{2.2}{\lambda }$
- $Δx=\frac{1.5}{\lambda }$

*Hint: The stability function for Euler's method is given by* $R(\lambda Δx)=1-\lambda Δx.$
:question/worked-solution:
A numerical method
${y}_{n+1}={y}_{n}+Δ{y}_{n}$
is stable for a given step size $Δx$ if, when applied to the test equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-\lambda y,\,y(0)=1,\,x\ge 0,\,\lambda >0,
$$

the numerical solution satisfies ${y}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty ,$ just like the exact solution.

For stability, we require that the following condition holds:

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(\lambda Δx)| & <1 \\ |1-\lambda Δx| & <1\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this gives

$$
0<\lambda Δx<2.
$$

This means that Euler's method is stable when applied to the test equation for values in the region $0<\lambda Δx<2.$

Now, we consider each step size in turn.

- For $Δx=\frac{0.25}{\lambda },$ we have $\lambda Δx=0.25.$ Since this value falls *within* the given region,

$$
\begin{aligned}0<\lambda Δx & <2 \\ 0<0.25 & <2,\end{aligned}
$$

Euler's method *must be* stable for this step size.

- For $Δx=\frac{3.5}{\lambda },$ we have $\lambda Δx=3.5\ge 2.$ Since this value falls *outside* the given region, Euler's method is *not* stable for this step size.

- For $Δx=\frac{2.2}{\lambda },$ we have $\lambda Δx=2.2\ge 2.$ Since this value falls *outside* the given region, Euler's method is *not* stable for this step size.

- For $Δx=\frac{1.5}{\lambda },$ we have $\lambda Δx=1.5.$ Since this value falls *within* the given region,

$$
\begin{aligned}0<\lambda Δx & <2 \\ 0<1.5 & <2,\end{aligned}
$$

Euler's method *must be* stable for this step size.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and IV only".

:question/problem:
$$

$$

Consider the differential equation above. Which of the following statements are true?

- ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{3x}$ is a solution to the equation.
- ${y}_{2}(x)={e}^{2x}$ is a solution to the equation.
- The functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation.
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that to determine whether $y(x)$ is a solution to the differential equation, we substitute $y$ and its derivatives into the equation. 

Let's check each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. We find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{1}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(x) & =3{e}^{3x} \\ {y}_{1}^{″}(x) & =9{e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{1}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{e}^{3x}-3(3{e}^{3x})+2({e}^{3x}) & =0 \\ 8 & =0\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{1}(x)$ is not a solution to the equation.

- Statement II is true. We find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{2}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′}(x) & =2{e}^{2x} \\ {y}_{2}^{″}(x) & =4{e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{2}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{e}^{2x}-3(2{e}^{2x})+2({e}^{2x}) & =0 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{2}(x)$ is a solution to the equation.

- Statement III is false. Since ${y}_{1}(x)$ is not a solution of the given differential equation, ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ don't form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

$$
\begin{aligned}9{e}^{3x-1}-6\cdot 3{e}^{3x-1}+9{e}^{3x-1} & =0 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}

$$

:question/problem:
$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-3x{y}^{′}+4y=0
$$

Consider the differential equation above. Which of the following statements are true?

- ${y}_{1}(x)={x}^{2}$ is a solution to the equation.
- ${y}_{2}(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)$ is a solution to the equation for $x>0.$
- The functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation on $(0,\infty ).$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that to determine whether $y(x)$ is a solution to the differential equation, we substitute $y$ and its derivatives into the equation. 

Let's check each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. First, we find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{1}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(x) & =2x \\ {y}_{1}^{″}(x) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{1}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot 2-3x\cdot 2x+4{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-6{x}^{2}+4{x}^{2} & =0 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{1}(x)$ is a solution to the equation.

- Statement II is true. First, we find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{2}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′}(x) & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+x \\ {y}_{2}^{″}(x) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{2}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+3)-3x(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+x)+4{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+3{x}^{2}-6{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)-3{x}^{2}+4{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) & =0 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{2}(x)$ is a solution to the equation.

- Statement III is true. Both ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of the equation. To check if these functions are linearly independent, we compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) \\ 2x & 2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+x\end{aligned}| \\  & ={x}^{2}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+x)-{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\cdot 2x \\  & =2{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+{x}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) \\  & ={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the  Wronskian is not identically $0$ on $(0,\infty ),$ the functions are linearly independent. Hence, ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation on $(0,\infty ).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III".

:question/problem:
For which of the following values is the Runge-Kutta Method (RK4) stable, given that $\lambda $ is the parameter of the test equation?

- $\lambda Δx=0.5$
- $\lambda Δx=1.5$
- $\lambda Δx=2.5$
- $\lambda Δx=3.2$

*Hint: The stability function $R$ of the RK4 method is given by*

$$
R(\lambda Δ)=1-\lambda Δx+\frac{(\lambda Δx)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(\lambda Δx)^{3}}{6}+\frac{(\lambda Δx)^{4}}{24}.
$$
:question/worked-solution:
A numerical method
${y}_{n+1}={y}_{n}+Δ{y}_{n}$
is stable for a given step size $Δx$ if, when applied to the test equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-\lambda y,\,y(0)=1,\,x\ge 0,\,\lambda >0,
$$

the numerical solution satisfies ${y}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty ,$ just like the exact solution.

When a method is applied to the test equation, the update takes the form

$$
{y}_{n+1}=R(\lambda Δx){y}_{n},
$$

where $R(\lambda Δx)$ is referred to as the stability function of the method. The set of values for which the method is stable, given by $|R(\lambda Δx)|<1,$ is called the stability region of the method.

The stability function of the RK4 Method is

$$
R(\lambda Δx)=1-\lambda Δx+\frac{(\lambda Δx)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(\lambda Δx)^{3}}{6}+\frac{(\lambda Δx)^{4}}{24}.
$$

Let's check the stability of the RK4 Method for each of the given values in turn.

- For $\lambda Δx=0.5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(0.5)| & =|1-0.5+\frac{(0.5)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(0.5)^{3}}{6}+\frac{(0.5)^{4}}{24}| \\  & =|\frac{233}{384}| \\  & =0.606…<1.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *within* the stability region, the RK4 Method is stable.

- For $\lambda Δx=1.5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(1.5)| & =|1-1.5+\frac{(1.5)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(1.5)^{3}}{6}+\frac{(1.5)^{4}}{24}| \\  & =|\frac{35}{128}| \\  & =0.273…<1.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *within* the stability region, the RK4 Method is stable.

- For $\lambda Δx=2.5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(2.5)| & =|1-2.5+\frac{(2.5)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(2.5)^{3}}{6}+\frac{(2.5)^{4}}{24}| \\  & =|\frac{83}{128}| \\  & =0.648…<1.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *within* the stability region, the RK4 Method is stable.

- For $\lambda Δx=3.2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(3)| & =|1-3.2+\frac{(3.2)^{2}}{2}-\frac{(3.2)^{3}}{6}+\frac{(3.2)^{4}}{24}| \\  & =|\frac{3427}{1875}| \\  & =1.827…<1.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *outside* the stability region, the RK4 Method is unstable.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only".

Note that the stability region of the RK4 Method is $0<\lambda Δx<2.785…,$ so it is not absolutely stable.

the numerical solution satisfies ${y}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty ,$ just like the exact solution.

- $Δx=2.2$ doesn't satisfy the inequality.

Therefore, Euler’s method is stable for step sizes $Δx=0.2$ and $Δx=0.45.$

Thus, the correct answer is "I and II only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Determining the Order of a Numerical Method Given the GTE or LTE

:question/problem:
Which of the following global truncation error expressions represent a fourth-order numerical method?

- $e(Δx)=4(Δx)^{4}+2(Δx)^{7}$
- $e(Δx)=11(Δx)^{5}+0.5(Δx)^{6}$
- $e(Δx)=0.2Δx+6(Δx)^{4}$
:question/worked-solution:
A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

With that in mind, let's check each option in turn:

:question/problem:
Suppose $f(x)={x}^{2}+3{x}^{4}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $f=O({x}^{2})$ as $x\to 0$
- $f=O({x}^{3})$ as $x\to 0$
- $f=O({x}^{4})$ as $x\to 0$
:question/worked-solution:
Suppose we wish to test whether the following statement is true:

$$
f(x)=O(g(x))\,\text{as}\,x\to a
$$

where $a$ is either finite or $+\infty .$ To do this, we can examine the following limit:

$$
{lim}_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}
$$

We have the following:

- If the limit is *finite*, the statement is true.

- If the limit is *infinite*, the statement is false.

- If the limit does not exist, the test is inconclusive.

Here, we must consider the function

$$
f(x)={x}^{2}+3{x}^{3}.
$$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Let $g(x)={x}^{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}+3{x}^{4}}{{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}(1+3{x}^{2}) \\  & =1+0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the limit is finite, and $f=O({x}^{2})$ as $x\to 0.$

- Statement II is false. Let $g(x)={x}^{3}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}+3{x}^{4}}{{x}^{3}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{1}{x}+3x)\end{aligned}
$$

As $x\to 0,$ the term $\frac{1}{x}$ becomes arbitrarily large in magnitude, while $3x\to 0.$
So

$$
{lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{1}{x}+3x)=\infty .
$$

Hence, the limit is infinite, and $f\ne O({x}^{3})$ as $x\to 0.$

- Statement III is false. Let $g(x)={x}^{4}.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}+3{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+3).\end{aligned}
$$

As $x\to 0,$ the term $\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}$ becomes arbitrarily large in magnitude, so

$$
{lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+3)=\infty .
$$

Hence, the limit is infinite, and $f\ne O({x}^{4})$ as $x\to 0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

To do this, we can examine the limit

$$
{lim}_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}.
$$

We have the following:

- If the limit is *finite*, the statement is true.

- If the limit is *infinite*, the statement is false.

- If the limit does not exist, the test is inconclusive.

Here, we must consider the polynomial

$$
f(x)=-5{x}^{6}+9{x}^{4}.
$$

Now, let us analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Let $g(x)=1.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(-5{x}^{6}+9{x}^{4}) \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

$$

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Proving the Smoothness Property

:question/problem:
Let $f(t)$ be a piecewise continuous function on $[0,\infty )$ with exponential order $a,$ and consider its Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)},\,s>a.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- If $f(t)$ is of exponential order $a,$ then the integral ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt$ converges for every $s>a.$
- If $f(t)$ is of exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform $F(s)$ exists for all $s>a.$
- The Laplace transform of any piecewise continuous function of exponential order is infinitely differentiable in its region of convergence.
:question/worked-solution:
If a function $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty )$ and has exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}
$$

exists for every real $s>a,$ and $F$ is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence.

The smoothness property states that, for each integer $n\ge 0$ and every $s>a,$

$$
{F}^{(n)}(s)=(-1)^{n}\,L{{t}^{n}f(t)}.
$$

Let's consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Since $f$ is of exponential order and is piecewise continuous, there exist constants $K,T>0$ and $a$ such that

$$
|f(t)|\le K{e}^{at},\,t>T.
$$

When computing the Laplace transform, we multiply $f(t)$ by ${e}^{-st}.$ If $s>a$, then for all sufficiently large $t$,

$$
|{e}^{-st}f(t)|\le K{e}^{-(s-a)t}.
$$

Because $s-a>0$, the function ${e}^{-(s-a)t}$ is integrable on $[T,\infty )$, and
$f$ is bounded on $[0,T].$
Therefore, the entire integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt
$$

converges.

- Statement II is true. The standard existence theorem for the Laplace transform says that if $f$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty )$ and of exponential order $a,$ then the improper integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt
$$

converges for every $s>a.$ This is exactly what it means for $F(s)$ to exist for all $s>a.$

- Statement III is true. The smoothness theorem guarantees

$$
{F}^{(n)}(s)=(-1)^{n}\,L{{t}^{n}f(t)}
$$

for every $n\ge 0$ and each $s>a,$ which shows that $F(s)$ is infinitely differentiable, even if $f(t)$ itself is not.

Therefore, the answer is "I, II, and III."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Applying the Limit Test

:question/problem:
Suppose $f(x)=3{x}^{2}-x.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $f=O(1)$ as $x\to \infty $
- $f=O(x{e}^{x})$ as $x\to \infty $
- $f=O({x}^{3})$ as $x\to \infty $
:question/worked-solution:
Suppose we wish to test whether the following statement is true:

$$
f(x)=O(g(x))\,\text{as}\,x\to a.
$$

To do this, we can examine the limit

$$
{lim}_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}.
$$

We have the following:

- If the limit is *finite*, the statement is true.

- If the limit is *infinite*, the statement is false.

- If the limit does not exist, the test is inconclusive.

Here, we must consider the polynomial

$$
f(x)=3{x}^{2}-x.
$$

Now, let us analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Let $g(x)=1.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(3{x}^{2}-x) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }x(3x-1) \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f\ne O(1)$ as $x\to \infty .$

- Statement II is true. Let $g(x)=x{e}^{x}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{3{x}^{2}-x}{x{e}^{x}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x(3x-1)}{x{e}^{x}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{3x-1}{{e}^{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since now direct evaluation leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{\infty }{\infty },$ we can evaluate the limit using L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{3x-1}{{e}^{x}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(3x-1)^{′}}{({e}^{x})^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{3}{{e}^{x}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f=O(x{e}^{x})$ as $x\to \infty .$

- Statement III is true. Let $g(x)={x}^{3}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{3{x}^{2}-x}{{x}^{3}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{3}{x}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f=O({x}^{8})$ as $x\to \infty .$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

:question/problem:
Suppose $f(x)={e}^{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $f=O(1)$ as $x\to \infty $
- $f=O(x)$ as $x\to \infty $
- $f=O({e}^{x})$ as $x\to \infty $
:question/worked-solution:
Suppose we wish to test whether the following statement is true:

$$
f(x)=O(g(x))\,\text{as}\,x\to a
$$

where $a$ is either finite or $+\infty .$ To do this, we can examine the following limit:

$$
{lim}_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}.
$$

We have the following:

- If the limit is *finite*, the statement is true.

- If the limit is *infinite*, the statement is false.

- If the limit does not exist, the test is inconclusive.

Here, we must consider the function

$$
f(x)={e}^{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x.
$$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Let $g(x)=1.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }({e}^{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f\ne O(1)$ as $x\to \infty .$

- Statement II is false. Let $g(x)=x.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{e}^{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since direct evaluation leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{\infty }{\infty },$ we can evaluate the limit using L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{e}^{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{({e}^{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{′}}{(x)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{({e}^{x}+\frac{1}{x})}{1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }({e}^{x}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\infty +0 \\  & =\infty \end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f\ne O(x)$ as $x\to \infty .$

- Statement III is true. Let $g(x)={e}^{x}.$ Then, using L'Hopital's rule where needed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{e}^{x}+\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{e}^{x}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(1+\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{e}^{x}}) \\  & =1+{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{e}^{x}} \\  & =1+{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{′}}{({e}^{x})^{′}} \\  & =1+{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1/x}{{e}^{x}} \\  & =1+{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{x{e}^{x}} \\  & =1+0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f=O({e}^{x})$ as $x\to \infty .$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Cases Where Differentiating Under the Integral Sign Applies

:question/problem:
For which of the following functions is it valid to differentiate under the integral sign?

- ${F}_{1}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{|x-t|}}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (0,1)$
- ${F}_{2}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{x}{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in R$
- ${F}_{3}(t)={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+x+t}\,\text{d}x,\,t\in (0,1)$
:question/worked-solution:
Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\times [c,d]$ and $\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function

$$
F(t)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x
$$

is differentiable on $(c,d),$ and

$$
{F}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\,\text{d}x.
$$

This is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*

With that in mind, let's check each function:

- For the first function, we have 

$$
{f}_{1}(x,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{|x-t|}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (0,1)$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d$ such that $[c,d]⊆(0,1),$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{1}$ is undefined when $x=t,$ since the denominator vanishes. Thus, ${f}_{1}$ is not continuous on $R,$ and differentiating under the integral sign is *not* valid.

- For the second function, we have 

$$
{f}_{2}(x,t)=\frac{x}{1+{t}^{2}}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in R$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{2}$ is continuous on $R.$ Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t}=-\frac{2tx}{(1+{t}^{2})^{2}}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{2}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t.$

- For the third function, we have 

$$
{f}_{3}(x,t)=\frac{1}{1+x+t}.
$$

We fix ${t}_{0}\in (0,1)$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d$ such that $[c,d]⊂(0,1),$ so $R=[0,1]\times [c,d].$

Note that ${f}_{3}$ is continuous on $R$ (since the denominator never vanishes on $R$). Computing the partial derivative, we have

$$
\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂t}=-\frac{1}{(1+x+t)^{2}}
$$

which exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{3}^{′}(t)$ for all $t\in (0,1).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying a Differential Equation Corresponding to a Phase Line

:question/problem:
![](images/96/96df34b3f844ee5abace182769011a3b4b2e413100fbca4cf25e829ca67948cc.png)

Consider the phase line shown above. Which of the following differential equations could have this phase line?

- $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(y-2)^{2}(y-4)$
- $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(y-2)(y-4)(y-6)$
- $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(y-2)^{2}(y-4)(y-6)$
:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that all three differential equations are of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y).
$$

The phase line gives us the following information:

- The equilibrium solutions are $y=2,$ $y=4$ and $y=6.$

- $f(y)$ is positive for $y\in (-\infty ,2)\cup (2,4)\cup (6,\infty ).$

- $f(y)$ is negative for $y\in (4,6).$

With this in mind, let's study each of the given equations.

- We start by considering

$$
{y}^{′}=(y-2)^{2}(y-4).
$$

In this case, $f(y)=(y-2)^{2}(y-4),$ and the equilibrium solutions are $y=2,4$ only.

Therefore, equation I does not have the given phase line.

- Next, we consider

$$
{y}^{′}=(y-2)(y-4)(y-6).
$$

In this case, $f(y)=(y-2)(y-4)(y-6),$ and the equilibrium solutions are $y=2,4,6.$

However, we note that $f(y)<0$ for $y\in (-\infty ,2).$ This does not correspond to the arrows shown on the phase line.

Therefore, equation II does not have the given phase line.

- Finally, we consider ${y}^{′}=(y-2)^{2}(y-4)(y-6).$

First, we see that $f(y)=(y-2)^{2}(y-4)(y-6),$ so $f(y)=0$ if $y=2,4,6.$ So, the equilibrium solutions correspond to those shown in the phase line.

Now, we can construct a sign table for $f(y)$ as follows:

|  | $(-\infty ,2)$ | $(2,4)$ | $(4,6)$ | $(6,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $(y-2)^{2}$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $y-4$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $y-6$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $f(y)$ | $+$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

So, we have that $f(y)$ is negative for $y\in (4,6),$ and $f(y)$ is positive for $y\in (-\infty ,2)\cup (2,4)\cup (6,\infty ).$
Therefore, equation III has the given phase line.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

:question/problem:
Which of the following equations is a d'Alembert differential equation?

- $y=x\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{′})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+({y}^{′})^{2})$
- $y{y}^{′}={x}^{3}y+1$
- $y-x({y}^{′})^{2}+{e}^{{y}^{′}}=0$
:question/worked-solution:
A differential equation is a d'Alembert differential equation if it can be expressed in the form

$$
y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}),
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are differentiable functions of ${y}^{′}.$ 

Note that, in the special case where $f({y}^{′})={y}^{′},$ the equation reduces to a Clairaut differential equation.

With that in mind, let's examine the given options.

- Equation I is a d'Alembert differential equation of the form $y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′})$ with 

$$
f({y}^{′})=\operatorname{cos}⁡({y}^{′}),\,g({y}^{′})=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+({y}^{′})^{2}).
$$

- Equation II is *not* a d'Alembert differential equation. Solving for $y,$ we get

$$
y=\frac{1}{{y}^{′}-{x}^{3}},
$$

which cannot be written in the form $y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}).$

- Equation III is a d'Alembert differential equation. Isolating the variable $y,$ we get

$$
y=x({y}^{′})^{2}-{e}^{{y}^{′}},
$$

which is of the form $y=xf({y}^{′})+g({y}^{′}).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

- ${D}_{1}(y)=(x-1)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy$
- ${D}_{2}(y)=y\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$
- ${D}_{3}(y)=4\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}-{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+xy$
:question/worked-solution:
An $n$th-order differential operator $L$ is linear if it is of the following form:

$$
L(y)={f}_{n}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{n}y}{\text{d}{x}^{n}}+{f}_{n-1}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{n-1}y}{\text{d}{x}^{n-1}}+⋯+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

where each ${f}_{i}$ is a function of $x$ only. 

With that in mind, let's check each operator.

- Operator ${D}_{1}$ is linear. It is a first-order linear differential operator of the form

$$
{D}_{1}(y)={f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

with ${f}_{1}(x)=x-1$ and ${f}_{0}(x)=2x.$

- Operator ${D}_{2}$ is *not* linear. The coefficient of the first term is $y,$ which depends on $y$ and therefore fails linearity.

- Operator ${D}_{3}$ is linear. It is a third-order linear differential operator of the form

$$
{D}_{3}(y)={f}_{3}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+{f}_{2}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

with ${f}_{3}(x)=4,{f}_{2}(x)=0,{f}_{1}(x)=-{x}^{2},$ and ${f}_{0}(x)=x.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function

:question/problem:
Let $F(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $\pi $-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $f(x+\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$
- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$
- $f(x)=f(x-2\pi )$ for all $x\in R$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $f$ is the $\pi $-periodic extension of $F,$ we have  

- $f(x+\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,\pi ).$

With that in mind, we examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $\pi $-periodicity: 

$$
f(x+\pi )=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is false. For example, take $x=\frac{3\pi }{2}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{3\pi }{2})=f(\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi )=f(\frac{\pi }{2})=F(\frac{\pi }{2})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=1,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{3\pi }{2})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x)\ne F(x)$ for $x=\frac{3\pi }{2}.$

- Statement III is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =f((x-\pi )+\pi ) \\  & =f(x-\pi ) \\  & =f((x-2\pi )+\pi ) \\  & =f(x-2\pi )\end{aligned}
$$

for all $x\in R.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

:question/problem:
Which of the following systems is an initial value problem?

- ${y}^{″}-3{y}^{′}+y={e}^{x},\,y(0)=1,\,y(2)=0$
- ${y}^{″}+4y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-1$
- ${y}^{″}-y={x}^{2}$
:question/worked-solution:
If a second-order differential equation for the function $y(x)$ is given with two conditions specified at the *same* location in the domain of $y,$ then this is an **initial value problem**.

Let's go through each equation in turn.

- The first system is not an initial value problem. It consists of a differential equation together with two conditions at different points in the domain of $y(x)$ (i.e., at $x=0$ and $x=2$). This is a **boundary value problem.**

- The second system is an initial value problem. The differential equation is together with two conditions at the same location in the domain of $y(x)$ (i.e., at $x=1$).

- The third system is not an initial value problem. It contains an equation only. No conditions are specified.

:question/problem:
Which of the following are first-order linear systems of ODEs?

- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)={x}_{1}(t){x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}$
- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=5{x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}^{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=6{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}$
- ${\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{3}{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t)+1 \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=\sqrt{7}\,{x}_{1}(t)+5{x}_{2}(t)+3t\end{aligned}$
:question/worked-solution:
A first-order linear system of differential equations with two dependent variables is a system of equations that takes the following standard form:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=a(t){x}_{1}(t)+b(t){x}_{2}(t)+f(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=c(t){x}_{1}(t)+d(t){x}_{2}(t)+g(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where

- $a(t),$ $b(t),$ $c(t),$ $d(t),$ $f(t),$ and $g(t)$ are known functions, and

- ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are unknown functions (dependent variables).

With this in mind, let's inspect each system:

- System I is not a first-order linear system of ODEs since it contains the term ${x}_{1}(t){x}_{2}(t).$

- System II is not a first-order linear system of ODEs since it contains the term ${x}_{2}^{2}(t).$

- System III is a first-order linear system of ODEs since it can be written in the standard form, where

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{3}, &  & b(t)=-2, &  & f(t)=1, \\ c(t)=\sqrt{7}, &  & d(t)=5, &  & g(t)=3t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function

:question/problem:
Let $F(x)=x$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $3$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,3)$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $f(x+6)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$
- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,3)$
- $f(x+1)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $f$ is the $3$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have 

- $f(x+3)=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,3).$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x+6)=f((x+3)+3)=f(x+3)=f(x),\end{aligned}
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is true by definition of the periodic extension.

- Statement III is false. For example, take $x=2.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2+1)=f(3)=F(3)=3,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2)=F(2)=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function

:question/problem:
Let $F(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $\frac{\pi }{2}$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(x)$ for all $x\in R$
- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in R$
- $f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(x-\frac{\pi }{2})$ for all $x\in R$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $f$ is the $\pi /2$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have  

- $f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$

With that in mind, we examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $\frac{\pi }{2}$-periodicity:

$$
f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in R.$

- Statement II is false. For example, take $x=\frac{3\pi }{4}.$ Using the periodicity of $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\frac{3\pi }{4})=f(\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(\frac{\pi }{4})=F(\frac{\pi }{4})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=1,\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{3\pi }{4})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{3\pi }{4})=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x)\ne F(x)$ for $x=\frac{3\pi }{4}.$

- Statement III is true. Since $f$ is $\frac{\pi }{2}$-periodic, any shift by a multiple of its period returns the same value:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(x)\,\text{and}\,f(x-\frac{\pi }{2})=f((x-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\pi }{2})=f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Since both sides equal $f(x),$ the statement is true for all $x\in R.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function

:question/problem:
Let $F(x)=cos\,(\frac{x}{2})$ for $x\in R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $2\pi $-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x\in [0,2\pi )$ to $x\in R.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- $f(x+2\pi )=f(x)$ for all $x\in R,$ and

- $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in [0,2\pi ).$

With that in mind, we examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
f(x+4\pi )=f((x+2\pi )+2\pi )=f(x+2\pi )=f(x)
$$

for all $x\in R.$

$$

- The vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are linearly independent.
- The vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are linearly dependent.
:question/worked-solution:
We say that three vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}=0
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

The equation ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ corresponds to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system, we create its augmented matrix and reduce it using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+5{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we conclude that the basic variables are ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$, while ${x}_{3}$ is the free variable. 

Since there is one free variable, the equation ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ has an infinite number of nonzero solutions, which means that the vectors are linearly dependent. 

Therefore, statements I and II are false, while statement III is true.

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)).

$$

From the matrix above, we conclude that the basic variables are ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$, while ${x}_{3}$ is the free variable. 

Since there is one free variable, the equation ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ has an infinite number of nonzero solutions, which means that the vectors are linearly dependent.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Linearly Independent and Dependent Sets Using Row Reduction

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: None of the statements are true

:question/problem:
Consider the following vectors:

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Assume that ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}$ are real numbers. Which of the following statements are true?

- The equation ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ has only the trivial solution ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$
- The vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are linearly dependent.
- The vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}$ are linearly independent.
:question/worked-solution:
We say that three vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}=0
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

The equation ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ corresponds to the system 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system, we create its augmented matrix and reduce it using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}+(0)=0\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=0
$$

and, substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}+(0)=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=0.
$$

Since ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0$, we get that the set ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is linearly independent.

Therefore, statements I and III are true, while statement II is false.

Which of the following statements are true?

- ${{b}_{3},{b}_{1},{b}_{1}+{b}_{3}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$
- ${x,{b}_{2},{c}_{1}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$
:question/worked-solution:
Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{3},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{2}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$, any vector of ${R}^{2},$ including the given vector $x,$ can be written as a linear combination of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ This means that ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2},x}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

- Statement II is false. The set ${{b}_{3},{b}_{1},{b}_{1}+{b}_{3}}$ is not a basis of ${R}^{3}$ because the third vector is a linear combination of ${b}_{3}$ and ${b}_{1}.$ This means that the set is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying the Dimension of the Null Space of Matrices Using Inspection

:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- If $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ then $\text{dim(Null}(A))=1.$
- If $B=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ then $\text{dim(Null}(B))=2.$
- If $C=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$ then $\text{dim(Null}(C))=3.$
:question/worked-solution:
The dimension of the null space of a matrix is the number of non-pivot columns in the matrix. 

Also, all of the given matrices are in row echelon form.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the statements.

- Statement I is true. The matrix $A$ has $1$ pivot column and $1$ non-pivot column. So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(A))=1.
$$

- Statement II is true. The matrix $B$ has $1$ pivot column and $2$ non-pivot columns (namely, the $2$nd and $3$rd columns). So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(B))=2.
$$

- Statement III is false. The matrix $C$ has $3$ pivot columns and no non-pivot columns. So, 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(C))=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

:question/worked-solution:
Since $B$ and $C$ are bases, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ and $C$ are maximally linearly independent sets in ${R}^{2}$ and ${R}^{3},$ respectively, and

- $B$ spans ${R}^{2},$ while $C$ spans ${R}^{3}.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}({b}_{2}+{b}_{3}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}){b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{2}+{b}_{3}}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{2}+{b}_{3}}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}={x}_{1}{b}_{1}+({x}_{2}-{x}_{3}){b}_{2}+{x}_{3}({b}_{2}+{b}_{3})
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(3{c}_{2})+{x}_{2}{c}_{1} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}(3{x}_{1}){c}_{2}+{x}_{2}{c}_{1} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, ${3{c}_{2},{c}_{1}}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of $C$ can be expressed as a linear combination of ${3{c}_{2},{c}_{1}}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{c}_{1}+{x}_{2}{c}_{2}={x}_{1}{c}_{1}+\frac{{x}_{2}}{3}(3{c}_{2})
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{3}$, any vector of ${R}^{3},$ including the given vector $x,$ can be written as a linear combination of ${b}_{1},$ ${b}_{2}$ and ${b}_{3}.$ This means that ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3},x}$ is linearly dependent and therefore, cannot be a basis.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

:question/problem:
Which of the following sets is a subspace of ${R}^{2}?$

- $A={⟨x,y⟩\in {R}^{2}:{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 0}$
- $B={⟨x,y⟩\in {R}^{2}:x=\frac{1}{2}y+2}$
- $C={0}$
:question/worked-solution:
Let's analyze each of the subsets.

- The set $A$ is a subspace. There is only one vector in ${R}^{2}$ that satisfies the equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 0,$ namely, the zero vector $0=⟨0,0⟩.$ So, $A={0}$, which is a special subspace of ${R}^{2}.$

- The set $B$ is not a subspace because it does not contain the zero vector. Indeed, $0=⟨0,0⟩$ does not satisfy the equation $x=\frac{1}{2}y+2$ since $0\ne \frac{1}{2}\cdot 0+2.$

- The set $C$ is a subspace. This subset has only one element, the zero vector $0=⟨0,0⟩,$ which is a special subspace of ${R}^{2}.$

So, the correct answer is "I and III only."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Sets Closed Under Addition and Scalar Multiplication

:answer-field/choices.:answer/value: None of the statements are true

:answer-field/correct.:answer/value: None of the statements are true

:question/problem:
Let $S$ be the set of all polynomials with real coefficients and whose degree is greater than or equal to $2.$  Which of the following statements are true? 

- $f(x)\in S,$ where $f(x)=2x.$
- For every $p(x),q(x)\in S,$ we have $p(x)+q(x)\in S.$
- The set is closed under addition.
:question/worked-solution:
Let's verify the statements one at a time.

- Statement I is false. The set $S$ contains only polynomials whose degree is greater than or equal to $2.$ However, 

$$
\operatorname{deg}⁡(2x)=1\ne 2.
$$

Therefore, $f(x)=2x\notin S.$

- Statement II is false. There exist functions in $S$ such that their sum is *not* in $S.$ For example, let $p(x)=x+{x}^{2}$ and $q(x)=x-{x}^{2}.$ Notice that both these functions belong to $S$ since $\operatorname{deg}⁡(p(x))=\operatorname{deg}⁡(q(x))=2\ge 2.$ However,

$$
\operatorname{deg}⁡(p(x)+q(x))=\operatorname{deg}⁡((x+{x}^{2})+(x-{x}^{2}))=\operatorname{deg}⁡(2x)=1≱2.
$$

Hence, $p(x)+q(x)\notin S.$

- Statement III is false. Since statement II is false, the set is *not* closed under addition.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying a True Statement Given a 2x2 Matrix

:question/problem:
Let 
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].$
Which of the following statements are true?

- $det(A)=0$
- $Ax=0$ has the unique  solution $⟨0,0⟩$
- $⟨5,-4⟩$ is a solution to $Ax=0$
:question/worked-solution:
Recall that given $A=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{aligned}]$, then according to the invertible matrix theorem the following statements are equivalent:    

- $A$ is invertible.

- The system $Ax=b$ has exactly one solution for any $2\times 1$ column vector $b.$

- The system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

- The lines ${a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y={b}_{1}$ and ${a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y={b}_{2}$ intersect at exactly one point.

- $det(A)\ne 0.$

With that in mind, let's now check our statements.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =det[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =3\cdot (-2)-2\cdot 0 \\  & =-6\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the fifth part of the invertible matrix theorem is true, all the other parts of the theorem are true too. Therefore, according to the theorem:

- Statement II is true by the third part of the invertible matrix theorem.

- Statement III is false. Again,  according to the third part of the invertible matrix theorem, the system $Ax=0$ has the unique zero solution.

Therefore, only statement II is true.

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements About Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $2.$
- If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2,$ then $-v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$
- $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $0.$
:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =2v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=2v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =2.$

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(-v)=-Av=-(2v)=2(-v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(-v)=2(-v),$ and $-v\ne 0,$ this implies that $-v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =2$ (but not $-2$).

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

- Statement III is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =0[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =0v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=0v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

:knowledge-point/_questions.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying True Statements About Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- If $v$ is an eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3$ then $v$ is also an eigenvector of the matrix ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =\frac{1}{3}.$
- An eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ is also an eigenvector of the inverse ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the same eigenvalue $\lambda =2.$
- If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3,$ then $5v$ is also an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda =-3.$
:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. By the definition of an eigenvector, we have 

$$
Av=3v.
$$

 
Multiplying it by ${A}^{-1}$ from the left, we obtain 

$$
v=3{A}^{-1}v.
$$

Dividing both sides by $3$, we get 

$$
{A}^{-1}v=\frac{1}{3}v.
$$

 
So, $v$ is an eigenvector  of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\frac{1}{3}.$

**Note:** In general, an eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to an eigenvalue $\lambda $ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\frac{1}{\lambda }.$

- Statement II is false. According to the statement above, an eigenvector of $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2$ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =\frac{1}{2}.$

- Statement III is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(5v)=5Av=5(-3v)=-3(5v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(5v)=-3(5v),$ and $5v\ne 0,$ this implies that $5v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-3.$

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

Which of the following statements are true?

- $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $4.$
:question/worked-solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(10v)=10Av=10(5v)=5(10v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(10v)=5(10v),$ and $10v\ne 0,$ this implies that $10v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =5.$

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 18\end{aligned}] \\  & =6[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =6v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=6v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =6.$

- Statement III is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =4v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=4v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =4.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III".

:question/problem:

- $C={6n:n\in N,1\le n\le 3}$
- $D={2n:n\in N,1\le n\le 4}$
:question/worked-solution:
First, we must find the elements of the sets $B,C$ and $D.$

- We find the elements of the set $B$ substituting the values $n\in {1,2,3,4}$ into the formula $3n,$ and we get the following elements:

$$
\begin{aligned}n=1 & \,⇒\,3(1)=3 \\ n=2 & \,⇒\,3(2)=6 \\ n=3 & \,⇒\,3(3)=9 \\ n=4 & \,⇒\,3(4)=12\end{aligned}
$$

So we have, $B={3,6,9,12}.$

- On the other hand, the elements of the set $C$ can be found substituting the values $n\in {1,2,3}$ into the formula $6n,$ and we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}n=1 & \,⇒\,6(1)=6 \\ n=2 & \,⇒\,6(2)=12 \\ n=3 & \,⇒\,6(3)=18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $C={6,12,18}.$

- Finally, the elements of the set $D$ can be found substituting the values $n\in {1,2,3,4}$ into the formula $2n,$ and we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}n=1 & \,⇒\,2(1)=2 \\ n=2 & \,⇒\,2(2)=4 \\ n=3 & \,⇒\,2(3)=6 \\ n=4 & \,⇒\,2(4)=8\end{aligned}
$$

So we have, $D={2,4,6,8}.$

Now, a set is a subset of $A$ if all of its elements are also elements of $A.$ With that in mind, let's inspect each option.

- $B={3,6,9,12}$ is a subset of $A.\,✓$

- $C={6,12,18}$ is a subset of $A.\,✓$

- $D={2,4,6,8}$ is *not* a subset of $A$ because it contains the element $2\notin A.\,\times $

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".
